docs.title: Each Task Runs Once
docs.text:
A task that several other tasks depend on runs the first time it is needed and is skipped after that:

class Tasks
  desc "Install gems"
  def setup = sh "bundle install"

  depends_on :setup
  desc "Run tests"
  def test = sh "rake test"

  depends_on :setup
  desc "Check style"
  def lint = sh "rubocop"

  depends_on [:test, :lint]
  desc "Test and lint (setup runs once)"
  def ci = puts "done"
end

asgard ci   # setup once, then test ∥ lint, then ci

Here test and lint start together and both want setup. One of them runs it; the other waits until it has finished rather than running it a second time or starting early. The guarantee holds across parallel groups, across files and across subcommands: one asgard command, one run per task.

docs.title: Transitive Dependencies
docs.text:
A prerequisite's own prerequisites run first, recursively:

class Tasks
  desc "Fetch gems"
  def setup = sh "bundle install"

  depends_on :setup
  desc "Compile assets"
  def build = sh "rake assets:precompile"

  desc "Check code style"
  def lint = sh "bundle exec rubocop"

  depends_on :build, :lint, :setup
  desc "Run the full pipeline"
  def ci = puts "Done."
end

asgard ci

setup          (as build's prerequisite)
  ↓
build
  ↓
lint
  ↓
(setup skipped: already done)
  ↓
ci

Tip

Declare a task where it logically belongs, as a prerequisite of the task that needs it. Naming it again further up is harmless (it runs once either way) but adds noise.

docs.title: Dependencies Across Files
docs.text:
All .loki files reopen the same Tasks class, so a task in one file may depend on a task in another. Names are checked once every file has loaded, so the order in which the files load does not matter:

# test.loki
class Tasks
  depends_on :build        # defined in build.loki, which may load before or after this file
  desc "Test"
  def test = sh "rake test"
end

# build.loki
class Tasks
  desc "Compile"
  def build = sh "rake build"
end

What does depend on load order is a task name defined twice: the later definition silently replaces the earlier one, including its depends_on. See Task Files and Help & Diagnostics for how asgard --doctor finds that.

docs.title: When a Dependency Fails
docs.text:
A failed prerequisite stops the run. How it stops depends on what failed:

  • A failing sh or shebang, or an abort, ends asgard with that command's exit status. The task that depended on it never starts. This is the normal case: asgard release with a failing test suite exits with the test runner's status.
  • An exception raised inside a dependency propagates and asgard reports it. Raise Asgard::Error for a clean one-line message: asgard: <message>, exit 1.
class Tasks
  desc "Refuse to deploy from a dirty tree"
  def clean_tree
    raise Asgard::Error, "commit or stash your changes first" unless `git status --porcelain`.strip.empty?
  end

  depends_on :clean_tree
  desc "Deploy to production"
  def deploy = sh "cap production deploy"
end

asgard deploy
# asgard: commit or stash your changes first
# (exit 1)

docs.title: A Return Value Never Stops Anything
docs.text: Only an exit or an exception stops a dependent task. A dependency that returns something, even :fail or false, has succeeded as far as the pipeline is concerned. (Returning :fail from the task you typed on the command line does make asgard exit 1, which is how the quality-gate pattern below reports failure, but it does not stop a task that depends on it.) To guard a task, raise or let a command fail. examples/confirm.loki in the repository is a guard task built this way: it asks "Really run asgard reset_database?" and raises Asgard::Error on anything but yes. See Examples.

docs.title: Failure in a Parallel Group
docs.text:
When one task in a parallel group fails, asgard waits for every other task in the group to finish before reporting, so no subprocess is left running on its own. One failure is reported the same way it would be on its own: a failing command exits asgard with its status, an exception propagates. When more than one task fails, each is named on stderr and the run ends with an error listing them:

asgard: dependency 'lint' failed: exit 1
asgard: dependency 'typecheck' failed: RuntimeError: boom
asgard: parallel dependencies failed: lint, typecheck

A task that is waiting for a shared prerequisite in another thread does not run if that prerequisite fails. With ci depending on [test, lint] and both depending on setup, a failing setup stops test, lint and ci alike, and asgard exits with setup's status.

docs.title: Passing Results Between Tasks
docs.text:
A task's return value is kept, and the task that depends on it can read it with dep_result. This is how a summary task collects what its prerequisites found. The example is the pattern the asgard repository uses for its own quality gates: every *_check task returns :pass, :fail, :warn or :skip, and quality prints a table:

class Tasks
  desc "Run the test suite"
  def test_check
    output = `bundle exec rake test 2>&1`
    File.write("test_output.txt", output)
    $?.success? ? :pass : :fail
  end

  desc "Check code style"
  def rubocop_check
    output = `bundle exec rubocop 2>&1`
    File.write("rubocop_output.txt", output)
    $?.success? ? :pass : :fail
  end

  depends_on [:test_check, :rubocop_check]
  desc "Run every check in parallel, then report"
  def quality
    dep_results.each { |name, status| puts "  #{status.to_s.upcase.ljust(5)} #{name}" }
    failed = dep_results.values.count(:fail)
    abort "#{failed} check(s) failed" unless failed.zero?
    puts "All checks passed."
  end
end

asgard quality

  PASS  test_check
  FAIL  rubocop_check
1 check(s) failed
  • dep_result(:test_check) is the return value of one direct dependency.
  • dep_results is a Hash of every direct dependency's name to its return value.

Both read the dependencies of the task that is running, not of tasks further down the chain. A check that uses backticks or system rather than sh can report its result as a value instead of ending asgard; see Exit on Failure.

Parallel dependencies do not share instance variables

Tasks in one parallel group each run on their own copy of the task object, so an @ivar set by a parallel dependency is not visible to the task that depends on it. Sequential dependencies do share it, which is why the difference can surprise you when a depends_on :a, :b later becomes depends_on [:a, :b]. Pass values with dep_result instead; examples/bad.loki in the repository shows the lost-update race that shared instance state produces.

docs.title: Startup Validation
docs.text:
Before any task runs, asgard checks every dependency list in every task class and stops with one line on the first problem. No backtrace, exit 1.

Circular dependencies

class Tasks
  depends_on :b
  desc "Task A"; def a = puts "a"

  depends_on :a
  desc "Task B"; def b = puts "b"
end

asgard a
# asgard: circular dependency — topological sort failed: [:a, :b]

A dependency that is not a task

asgard ci
# asgard: undefined task(s) in depends_on: ghost_check

A private method is not a task, so depends_on :my_helper is undefined even though the method exists. Make it a task or call it from the task body.

A depends_on with nothing after it

A depends_on at the end of a class body, or followed only by private methods, has no task to attach to:

asgard
# asgard: depends_on(build, test) declared without a following task definition

A dependency that needs arguments

A task with required positional parameters cannot be a dependency, because nothing would supply them:

desc "greet NAME", "Greet NAME"
def greet(name) = puts "Hello, #{name}"

depends_on :greet
desc "Welcome"
def welcome = puts "welcome"

asgard welcome
# asgard: task 'greet' has 1 required argument(s) and cannot be used as a dependency

Give the parameter a default (def greet(name = "World")) or read the value from an option or environment variable instead.

asgard --doctor reports the same problems without stopping at the first one; see Help & Diagnostics.

docs.title: Dynamic Dependencies
docs.text:
A plain depends_on list is fixed when you write it. Sometimes the list has to be discovered: "every task whose name ends in _check", wherever it is defined, including a file that is only imported on some machines. For that, give depends_on a block, or a lambda, instead of a list. It is called once, after every .loki file has loaded, and must return the same shape a plain list would be:

depends_on { [all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).sort.map(&:to_sym)] }
desc "Run every *_check task in parallel, then report"
def quality
  dep_results.each { |name, status| puts "#{status} #{name}" }
end

depends_on -> { [all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).sort.map(&:to_sym)] }
desc "The same thing, written as a lambda"
def quality2 = puts "done"

all_commands.keys is the list of every task name defined so far, as strings. The block above returns [[:a_check, :b_check, :c_check]]: an array with one element, an array of three tasks, which is one parallel stage, exactly like writing depends_on [:a_check, :b_check, :c_check].

docs.title: The Shape of the Result
docs.text:
The block must return an Array of stages. Each stage is a Symbol or String (a sequential task) or an Array of Symbols or Strings (a parallel group). Nothing nests deeper than that. A mixed pipeline is written the same way the plain form is:

depends_on { [:setup, %i[a_check b_check], :teardown] }
desc "setup, then a_check and b_check in parallel, then teardown"
def full_cycle = puts "full_cycle: done"

Use braces for a one-line block and do ... end when the block has several statements. Either way the last expression is the result:

depends_on do
  all_checks  = all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).sort.map(&:to_sym)
  slow_checks = %i[integration_check]

  [:setup, all_checks - slow_checks, :teardown]
end
desc "Every check except the slow ones"
def smoke = puts "smoke: done"

The shape is checked as soon as the block returns. A wrong shape stops asgard with a message naming the task and the offending value, instead of failing later with an obscure error. The common mistake is one pair of brackets too many:

depends_on { [[all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).map(&:to_sym)]] }   # one [ ] too many

asgard: depends_on proc/block for 'quality' returned invalid dependency [:a_check, :b_check, :c_check] (Array) in a parallel group; expected a Symbol or String

Other shape errors read the same way, for example returned invalid stage 123 (Integer); expected a Symbol, String, or Array of them. If the block itself raises, asgard reports that too: asgard: depends_on proc for 'quality' raised RuntimeError: boom.

docs.title: What the Block Can See
docs.text:
The block is written in the Tasks class body, so inside it self is that class: all_commands and the other class-level words work bare, with no prefix, even though the block is not called until later. Once it resolves, the result replaces the block, so cycle detection, the undefined-task check and the arguments check all run against the resolved list, exactly as for a plain one.

depends_on takes a list or a block, never both; combining them is an error.

Warning

The block runs before the command line is parsed, so options, verbose? and debug? inside it always see their defaults, never what was typed on this run. Keep the block to shaping the dependency list.

Tip

Reach for the block only when the list cannot be known until every file has loaded. A fixed list is clearer written out. examples/depends_on_block/good/.loki and bad/.loki in the repository are two small projects showing the block form working and the shape error; see Examples.

docs.title: Dependencies Inside Subcommands
docs.text:
depends_on works inside a subcommand class exactly as at the top level. It names that class's own tasks:

class DBCommands < Tasks
  desc "Run migrations"
  def migrate = sh "rails db:migrate"

  desc "Load seed data"
  def seed = sh "rails db:seed"

  depends_on :migrate, :seed
  desc "Migrate then seed"
  def reset = puts "Done."
end

class Tasks
  desc "db SUBCOMMAND", "Manage the database"
  subcommand "db", DBCommands
end

asgard db reset   # migrate → seed → reset

Each subcommand class has its own dependency graph, validated at startup like the top-level one. See Subcommands.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Form Meaning depends_on :a Run a first depends_on :a, :b Run a, then b depends_on [:a, :b] Run a and b at the same time depends_on :a, [:b, :c], :d a, then b with c, then d depends_on { [...] } or depends_on -> { [...] } Compute the list after every file has loaded dep_result(:a) In the task body: what a returned dep_results In the task body: every direct dependency's result, by name

Every task runs once per asgard command. A failing command or a raised error stops the run; a return value does not.

docs.title: Help & Diagnostics
docs.text:
This page is about finding out what asgard knows and why something did not work: the help pages, the command tree, the text you can add above and below them, the --doctor report, and every error asgard prints at startup, with its exit status.

Start with the two commands you will use most:

asgard help          # every task, with its description
asgard --doctor      # which files loaded, which tasks each defines, what is wrong

docs.title: asgard help
docs.text:
asgard help (or asgard with no arguments, when no default_task is set) lists every task that has a desc, the built-in groups, and the options every task accepts:

asgard v0.6.0 The Mighty Thor and Loki working for you

Commands:
  asgard build                # Compile the project
  asgard deploy ENV           # Deploy to ENV
  asgard help [COMMAND]       # Describe available commands or one specific command
  asgard jobs SUBCOMMAND      # List, stop and restart the background jobs started with `sh ..., background: true`
  asgard schedule SUBCOMMAND  # Manage schedules declared with `schedule :task, ...` (launchd on macOS, systemd on Linux)
  asgard test                 # Run the test suite
  asgard tree                 # Print a tree of all available commands
  asgard watcher SUBCOMMAND   # Run and manage the file watcher declared with `watch :task, paths: ...`

Options:
  [--debug]    # Enable debug mode ($DEBUG = true)
               # Default: false
  [--verbose]  # Enable verbose output ($VERBOSE = true)
               # Default: false
  [--version]  # Show asgard version and exit
               # Default: false
  [--doctor]   # Diagnose .loki resolution, imports, and task definitions for the CWD, then exit
               # Default: false

Documentation ... https://madbomber.github.io/asgard
Github Repo ..... https://github.com/MadBomber/asgard

The first line and the last two are asgard's own header and footer. Yours go between them; see header and footer. A task defined without a desc, or with desc "...", hide: true, is left out of the list but still runs.

asgard help TASK shows one task: its usage line with positional parameters, its own options followed by the shared ones, and its long_desc when it has one:

asgard help deploy

Usage:
  asgard deploy ENV

Options:
  -b, [--branch=BRANCH]          # Git branch to deploy
                                 # Default: main
  -n, [--dry-run], [--no-dry-run], [--skip-dry-run]  # Print commands without running
  [--debug]                      # Enable debug mode ($DEBUG = true)
  ...

Deploy ENV

Per-task help does not show the header or footer. For a subcommand group, asgard help db, asgard db help and asgard db help migrate all work; see Subcommands.

Tip

Put asgard's options after the task name: asgard build --verbose. Written before it, asgard --verbose build is read as asgard help build. The two flags that answer and exit, --version and --doctor, are the exception and go first.

docs.title: asgard tree
docs.text:
asgard tree prints the commands as a tree: the top-level tasks first, with each subcommand group as one leaf, then one section per group listing its own tasks. Header and footer are shown, as on help:

asgard tree

asgard v0.6.0 The Mighty Thor and Loki working for you

tasks
  ├─ _jobs (List, stop and restart the background jobs started with `sh ..., background: true`)
  ├─ _schedule (Manage schedules declared with `schedule :task, ...` (launchd on macOS, systemd on Linux))
  ├─ _watcher (Run and manage the file watcher declared with `watch :task, paths: ...`)
  ├─ build (Compile the project)
  ├─ db (Manage the database)
  └─ deploy (Deploy to ENV)
  schedule
    ├─ install (Install this project's schedule declarations (removes undeclared ones))
    ├─ list (Show this project's installed entries, their state, and last exit status)
    ...
  watcher
    ...
  jobs
    ...
  d_b_commands
    ├─ migrate (Run pending migrations)
    └─ seed (Load seed data)

The built-in groups appear as leaves under their reserved names (_jobs, _schedule, _watcher) and as sections under the names you type (jobs, schedule, watcher). A group of your own gets a section named after its class, so DBCommands shows as d_b_commands.

docs.title: header and footer
docs.text:
header "text" and footer "text" in the class body add lines above the command list and below the options block on asgard help and asgard tree:

class Tasks
  header "my-project: build and release tasks"
  footer "See https://example.com/docs for details"
end

Both may be called more than once, and from more than one file. Every call is kept. The difference is the order:

  • header appends. Each call goes below the previous ones, so the first file to call it (usually .loki) stays at the top.
  • footer prepends. Each call goes above the previous ones, so text from a file that loads later sits closer to the commands.
# .loki
class Tasks
  header "my-project"
  footer "Maintainer: you@example.com"
end
import "deploy.loki"

# deploy.loki
class Tasks
  header "  deploy targets: staging, production"
  footer "See runbook at wiki/deploy"
end

asgard v0.6.0 The Mighty Thor and Loki working for you

my-project

  deploy targets: staging, production

Commands:
  asgard deploy  # Deploy
  ...

Options:
  ...

See runbook at wiki/deploy

Maintainer: you@example.com

Documentation ... https://madbomber.github.io/asgard
Github Repo ..... https://github.com/MadBomber/asgard

Each call is separated from the next by a blank line. A multi-line heredoc counts as one call, so lines that belong together go in one heredoc.

A header that needs a computed value uses helper, which defines a method usable in the class body. This is how asgard's own .loki prints its version and root:

class Tasks
  @@project ||= "asgard".freeze

  helper(:project_version) do
    @@project_version ||= File.read("lib/#{@@project}/version.rb").match(/VERSION\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/)[1].freeze
  end

  header <<~HEAD
    Project:  #{@@project} (v#{project_version})
    Root Dir: #{loki_up.parent}
    Default task: #{default_task}
  HEAD
end

See Helper Methods.

docs.title: The Doctor Report
docs.text:
asgard --doctor loads the task files the way a normal run would, but instead of running a task it reports what it found. Reach for it when:

  • a task you defined does not show up, or runs something other than what its file says
  • asgard reports a dependency error and you want to see every definition involved
  • an import seems to load nothing
  • you suspect a .loki higher up the tree is being used instead of the one you expect

It also works when a normal run cannot start at all, because a file is broken or a dependency graph has a cycle. That is the point: it tells you where, instead of stopping.

asgard --doctor

asgard doctor -- /Users/you/myproject
============================================================
  [INFO] using .loki marker: /Users/you/myproject/.loki
  [WARN] shadowed marker (never reached): /Users/you/.loki
  [INFO] import "quality.loki" -> /Users/you/myproject/quality.loki
  [INFO] import "gem_tasks.loki" -> /Users/you/myproject/gem_tasks.loki
  [INFO] import "local.loki" -- nothing new (not found or already loaded)

Tasks by file:

  .loki
    deploy  .loki:12
    where   .loki:18   hidden (no desc; not shown by help)

  quality.loki
    test_check     quality.loki:11
    rubocop_check  quality.loki:39
    quality        quality.loki:30

  gem_tasks.loki
    build    gem_tasks.loki:16
    release  gem_tasks.loki:31
============================================================
No problems found (1 warning(s)).

docs.title: Reading the Report
docs.text:
Line Meaning [INFO] using .loki marker: ... The .loki a run from this directory uses [WARN] shadowed marker (never reached): ... Another .loki further up the tree. Harmless, but if you expected that one to be used, this is why it is not [INFO] import "x" -> /path/a.loki, /path/b.loki What each import and import_up loaded, in order, including imports made by imported files [INFO] import "x" -- nothing new (not found or already loaded) A glob that matched nothing, or a file that an earlier import already loaded [FAIL] load failed: NoMethodError: ... A task file raised while loading. The normal run would stop with the same message [FAIL] Tasks dependency graph: ... A cycle, an undefined dependency, or another graph problem, in the named class

Tasks by file lists every task under the file that defines it, as name file:line, a form most editors can jump to. A file that only imports others says (no tasks defined — imports only). Two notes can follow a task:

  • hidden (no desc; not shown by help): a public method without a desc. It runs from the command line and as a dependency, but help leaves it out. If it was meant as a helper, make it private, put it in no_commands, or use helper. See Defining Tasks.
  • OVERRIDDEN by file:line — never callable and active — redefines file:line: the same task name defined twice. Only the last definition exists; the earlier one is dead. Each overridden task counts as one problem in the summary.

The summary line is No problems found., No problems found (N warning(s)). or N problem(s), M warning(s).

docs.title: A Deliberate Override
docs.text:
The asgard repository ships an example. xyzzy.loki defines a xyzzy task, and the root .loki, which imports it, defines xyzzy again. Run asgard --doctor from a clone:

asgard doctor -- /Users/you/asgard
============================================================
  [INFO] using .loki marker: /Users/you/asgard/.loki
  [INFO] import "quality.loki" -> /Users/you/asgard/quality.loki
  [INFO] import "gem_tasks.loki" -> /Users/you/asgard/gem_tasks.loki
  [INFO] import "git.loki" -> /Users/you/asgard/git.loki
  [INFO] import "doc_tasks.loki" -> /Users/you/asgard/doc_tasks.loki
  [INFO] import "xyzzy.loki" -> /Users/you/asgard/xyzzy.loki

Tasks by file:

  .loki
    xyzzy  .loki:26   active — redefines xyzzy.loki:6

  quality.loki
    test_check     quality.loki:11
    test_verbose   quality.loki:21
    quality        quality.loki:30
    rubocop_check  quality.loki:39
    ...

  xyzzy.loki
    xyzzy  xyzzy.loki:6   OVERRIDDEN by .loki:26 — never callable
============================================================
1 problem(s), 0 warning(s).

docs.title: When the Files Do Not Load
docs.text:
A broken file still gets a report. The load failure is the finding, and there is no task listing because nothing finished loading:

asgard doctor -- /Users/you/myproject
============================================================
  [INFO] using .loki marker: /Users/you/myproject/.loki
  [FAIL] load failed: NoMethodError: undefined method 'dependz_on' for class Tasks
============================================================
1 problem(s), 0 warning(s).

A dependency problem, on the other hand, loads fine, so the listing is there to help you find the definitions:

  [FAIL] Tasks dependency graph: topological sort failed: [:a, :b]

Tasks by file:

  .loki
    a  .loki:3
    b  .loki:5

docs.title: Load Errors
docs.text:
A task file that raises while loading stops asgard with one line: where, what, and the error class. The location is the nearest line inside a .loki file.

A typo in a DSL word:

asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:2: undefined method 'dependz_on' for class Tasks (NoMethodError)

A syntax error (the location comes from Ruby's own message):

asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:4: syntax error found (SyntaxError)

A shell whose executable does not exist:

asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:2: shell :bash: /nope/bash is not an executable file (ArgumentError)

An import of a file that is not there:

asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:1: cannot load such file -- /Users/you/myproject/missing.loki (LoadError)

When one line is not enough, set ASGARD_TRACE to get the whole backtrace, including Ruby's "Did you mean?" suggestion:

ASGARD_TRACE=1 asgard help

/Users/you/myproject/.loki:2:in '<class:Tasks>': undefined method 'dependz_on' for class Tasks (NoMethodError)
Did you mean?  depends_on
    from /Users/you/myproject/.loki:1:in '<top (required)>'
    ...

docs.title: Startup Validation Errors
docs.text:
After every file has loaded, and before any task runs, asgard checks the dependency graph and the declarations. Each problem is one line and exit status 1.

Problem Message Two tasks depend on each other, directly or through others asgard: circular dependency — topological sort failed: [:a, :b] A depends_on names a task that does not exist asgard: undefined task(s) in depends_on: ghost A depends_on with no def after it (at the end of a class body) asgard: depends_on(a) declared without a following task definition A dependency takes a required argument asgard: task 'b' has 1 required argument(s) and cannot be used as a dependency A block-form depends_on returned the wrong shape asgard: depends_on proc/block for 'quality' returned invalid stage 123 (Integer); expected a Symbol, String, or Array of them A block-form depends_on raised asgard: depends_on proc for 'quality' raised RuntimeError: boom A task or helper uses a name asgard's command machinery needs (shell, options, invoke, run, args, ...) asgard: 'args' at /Users/you/myproject/.loki:3 is a name Thor reserves and cannot be a task or helper; rename it Two different schedule declarations under one name asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:4: schedule: "a" is already declared; give one a distinct as: name (ArgumentError) Two different watch declarations under one name asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:4: watch: "a" is already declared; give one a distinct as: name (ArgumentError)

The last three are raised while the file loads, so they carry a file and line like any load error. asgard --doctor reports the dependency ones under Tasks dependency graph, with the task listing beneath, and the others as load failed.

docs.title: Runtime Errors
docs.text:
Once a task is running, three kinds of error end the run:

An error you raise. raise Asgard::Error, "message" inside a task prints asgard: message and exits 1, with no backtrace. It is the right way for a task, or a dependency, to refuse to go on:

class Tasks
  desc "Deploy to production"
  def deploy
    raise Asgard::Error, "working tree is not clean" unless `git status --porcelain`.empty?
    sh "cap production deploy"
  end
end

asgard: working tree is not clean

Any other exception prints Ruby's usual message and backtrace.

A failing command. When a sh or shebang script exits non-zero, asgard exits with that status at once. Nothing after the call runs. See Shell Commands.

A usage error. A missing argument, an unknown option, an unknown command or an ambiguous abbreviation prints a one-line message and exits 1:

Could not find command "nope".
Ambiguous command test matches [test_check, test_verbose]
asgard: unknown command '_version'

The last one is asgard refusing a name that starts with _, which is reserved for its built-ins.

docs.title: Exit Status
docs.text:
Status When 0 The task finished, and did not return :fail 1 The task returned the symbol :fail; a usage error; a load or validation error; Asgard::Error was raised; a parallel dependency group had failures The command's own status A sh or shebang script exited non-zero: asgard exits with the same number 127 The interpreter a shebang names is not on PATH (asgard: shell :lua not found: lua ...) 128 + N The script was ended by signal N (143 after a TERM, 137 after a KILL), as a shell would report it 130 You pressed Ctrl-C

A task that wants to report failure without stopping on the spot, the way asgard's own *_check quality gates do, returns :fail. Any other return value, including :warn and :skip, is a success. See Dependencies for passing results between tasks.

docs.title: --debug and --verbose
docs.text:
Both flags set a Ruby global before the task runs, which your tasks read through debug? and verbose? (see Options & Flags). They also make asgard say a little more:

  • --verbose prints each file an import loads from inside a task body: import: /path/to/file.loki.
  • --debug with --verbose also prints import: skip /path (already loaded) and import_up: name not found.

Imports at the top of .loki run before the flags are read. To trace those, use Ruby's own warning switch or --doctor:

RUBYOPT=-w asgard build     # import: ... for every file as it loads
asgard --doctor             # the same chain, without running anything

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Tasks read configuration from the environment all the time: a port, a deploy target, an API key. This page covers how a task reads a variable, how a project loads a .env file, and then the part that is easy to miss: the variables asgard itself sets for the processes it starts, and the few it reads.

The short version:

class Tasks
  dotenv                     # load .env, if there is one

  desc "Start the server"
  def start = sh "puma -p #{env(:port, '3000')}"
end

asgard start               # puma -p 3000
PORT=8080 asgard start     # puma -p 8080

docs.title: Reading Variables with env
docs.text:
env fetches an environment variable by name. The name may be a symbol or a string, and it is upcased for you, so env(:port) and env("PORT") are the same call.

Call Behaviour env(:port, "3000") The value of PORT, or "3000" when it is unset env(:api_key) The value of API_KEY; raises KeyError when it is unset env("DATABASE_URL") A string name works the same way env("database_url") Lower case is upcased: still DATABASE_URL

Use the no-default form for anything a task cannot run without. The error names the variable, and asgard stops before the task does half its work:

class Tasks
  desc "Deploy the app"
  def deploy = sh "cap #{env(:deploy_target)} deploy"
end

asgard deploy
# .loki:3:in 'deploy': key not found: "DEPLOY_TARGET" (KeyError)

Note

Environment values are always strings. Convert where it matters: env(:port, "3000").to_i, env(:debug, "false") == "true".

env is available everywhere in a .loki file: in task bodies, in helpers, and in the class body (@@host ||= env(:host, "localhost")).

docs.title: Loading .env Files with dotenv
docs.text:
dotenv loads a file of KEY=value lines into the environment before any task runs. Call it in the class body, not inside a task:

class Tasks
  dotenv                  # loads .env

  desc "Print the app name from .env"
  def check = puts env(:app_name)
end

# .env
APP_NAME=myapp
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/myapp_development
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0
PORT=3000

docs.title: A Named File, or Several
docs.text:
class Tasks
  dotenv                  # .env: shared defaults
  dotenv ".env.local"     # per-machine values
end

Each call adds the variables it finds. A variable that is already set, by an earlier dotenv call or by your shell, is never overwritten. That is the standard dotenv rule, and it means your shell always has the last word: PORT=8080 asgard start beats whatever .env says.

docs.title: A Missing File Is Not an Error
docs.text: dotenv checks that the file exists and does nothing when it does not. A .loki can name .env.local without requiring every developer to create one.

docs.title: From Any Subdirectory
docs.text:
The path is relative to the directory you ran asgard from, not to .loki. Run asgard start from src/app/ and a bare dotenv looks for src/app/.env, finds nothing, and silently loads nothing. Ask for the nearest .env up the tree instead:

class Tasks
  dotenv loki_up(".env") || ".env"
end

loki_up(".env") returns the first .env found in the current directory or any ancestor, and the || ".env" keeps the usual no-op behaviour when there is none. See Task Files.

docs.title: File Format
docs.text: Standard dotenv syntax: one KEY=value per line, # comments, quoted values when a value has spaces, and ${OTHER} to reference another variable. Multi-line values are supported as the dotenv gem documents them.

docs.title: One Value, Several Tasks
docs.text:
When several tasks read the same variable, read it once in a private helper so the default lives in one place:

class Tasks
  dotenv

  desc "Start the server"
  def start = sh "puma -p #{port}"

  desc "Show the configuration"
  def config = puts "listening on #{port}"

  private

  def port = env(:port, "3000").to_i
end

For a value that is also needed in the class body (a header line, say), use helper instead of private; see Helper Methods.

docs.title: Variables Asgard Sets
docs.text: Three of asgard's built-ins start tasks as new processes: the watcher, background jobs and schedules. Each hands its process a specific environment, and a few ASGARD_* variables that tell the task why it is running.

docs.title: Tasks Run by the Watcher
docs.text:
A task the watcher triggers does not inherit the shell the watcher was started from. It gets:

Layer Contents A fixed base PATH, HOME, USER, LOGNAME, SHELL, LANG, every LC_*, TMPDIR, SSH_AUTH_SOCK, and the Ruby setup the watcher started under: GEM_HOME, GEM_PATH, RUBYOPT, RUBYLIB, every BUNDLE_* and BUNDLER_*. All captured when asgard watcher start ran The declaration's env: watch :docs, paths: "docs", env: { BUILD_ENV: "dev" } adds BUILD_ENV=dev .envrc Loaded in the task's own process through direnv exec when direnv is on PATH (see .envrc and direnv) .env Only if your .loki calls dotenv, as it would for any run The trigger ASGARD_WATCH, the entry name; ASGARD_WATCH_ROOT, the project root; and the changed paths, below

The changed paths arrive in three variables, one path per line, relative to the project root:

Variable Contents ASGARD_MODIFIED Files whose contents changed ASGARD_ADDED Files that appeared ASGARD_REMOVED Files that disappeared ASGARD_CHANGES_FILE Set instead of the three above when the lists are too large for the environment (over 128 KB, as a branch switch under a ** watch can produce). It names a JSON file holding the same three lists

You do not read these yourself. The changes method does, from whichever form they came in, and returns .modified, .added, .removed and .all; every list is empty when you run the task by hand. See Watched Files.

asgard watcher preview prints the exact command and environment each entry would run, so there is never any guessing about what a triggered task sees.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
A job started with sh "...", background: true inherits the full environment of the task that started it, plus:

Variable Contents ASGARD_JOB The job's name (doc_server-1, api) ASGARD_JOB_STATUS The file the job's exit status is written to when it ends PYTHONUNBUFFERED Set to 1 unless you set it yourself. Python fully buffers stdout when it is a file, so without this a print loop would show nothing in the job's log until the process exits

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
A job installed by asgard schedule install runs under launchd or systemd, far from any shell of yours. It gets:

Layer Contents PATH The PATH that was current when you ran install. Change your PATH and re-run install to update it The declaration's env: schedule :sync, every: 3600, env: { "SYNC_TARGET" => "s3://bucket" }. The values are written into the job file, which only your user can read .envrc Loaded at run time through direnv exec when direnv is on PATH .env Only if your .loki calls dotenv

Nothing else. In particular, variables you exported in .zshrc or .bashrc are not there, and neither is Homebrew's PATH on a Mac unless it was in PATH at install time. asgard schedule preview shows the job files, environment included, before you install them.

docs.title: Variables Asgard Reads
docs.text:
Variable Effect ASGARD_TRACE When set, a task file that fails to load prints the full Ruby backtrace instead of asgard's one-line summary. See Help & Diagnostics ASGARD_LOG_MAX Bytes the watcher's log may reach before it is rotated to watcher.log.1. Default 10 MB XDG_STATE_HOME Where per-project state lives (watcher and job records, logs). Default ~/.local/state; asgard uses <XDG_STATE_HOME>/asgard/ XDG_CONFIG_HOME On Linux, where systemd user units are written. Default ~/.config COLUMNS The width the list tables wrap to when output is not a terminal (piped to a file or less). Default 120 NO_COLOR When set, the list tables print without colour

See Files & Directories for the paths these produce.

docs.title: .envrc and direnv
docs.text:
If the project root has a .envrc, asgard's watcher and schedules wrap each task in direnv exec <root>. The task's own process then loads .envrc the way your shell does when you cd into the project: API keys and other secrets reach the task at run time and are never copied into a launchd plist, a systemd unit or a watcher record. A rotated key takes effect on the next run with nothing to reinstall.

For that to work, direnv has to be on PATH when you run asgard schedule install or asgard watcher start. When it is not, each prints a warning and goes on without it:

schedule: .envrc found but direnv is not on PATH; its variables will not be loaded
watcher: .envrc found but direnv is not on PATH; its variables will not be loaded

A task you run by hand from a direnv-enabled shell already has .envrc loaded, so nothing changes there.

docs.title: PATH Is Not the Same Everywhere
docs.text:
The PATH in your terminal is built by your shell's startup files. A task that runs under launchd, systemd or the watcher never runs those files. The practical consequences:

  • A tool on your terminal's PATH may be missing in a scheduled run. Homebrew's /opt/homebrew/bin is the usual example on a Mac. Schedules capture PATH at install time, so run install from a shell that has what the task needs. The watcher captures PATH at start.
  • The same name can be a different program. bash in a Homebrew terminal is 5.x; under launchd it is the 3.2 build in /bin. A script that uses bash 4 syntax passes by hand and fails on a schedule.

Pin the executables that matter in the shells registry, so every run uses the same one:

class Tasks
  shell :bash, "/opt/homebrew/bin/bash"
end

See Shell Commands.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The asgard repository ships working .loki files in its examples/ directory, one for each feature, plus the gem's own task files at the repository root, which are a real multi-file project in daily use. This page says what each one shows and how to run it. Copy whatever is useful into your own project.

docs.title: Running the Examples Directory
docs.text:
examples/ has its own .loki, so it is a project in its own right:

git clone https://github.com/MadBomber/asgard.git
cd asgard/examples
asgard help

Its .loki loads everything else explicitly:

# examples/.loki
import "*.loki"                      # every sibling task file, alphabetically
import "subdir/import_demo.loki"     # one file from a subdirectory

Three examples are separate projects with their own .loki and must be run from their own directory: depends_on_block/good, depends_on_block/bad and watcher_examples.

Note

concurrent.loki and bad.loki exist to be run, not read: their point is output that changes from run to run.

docs.title: kitchen_sink.loki
docs.text:
Every Thor word and most of asgard's, in one file. Task names avoid the gem's own (test, build, quality, install, release) so the file can sit beside them.

  • @@app_name and @@build_dir class variables shared by every task
  • private computed values (version, sha, branch) with memoization
  • class_option :dry_run and class_option :env with enum, on every task
  • default_task :greet and map aliases (g, ck, rp, pl)
  • A positional parameter with a default (hello NAME)
  • All five option types (:string, :boolean, :numeric, :array, :hash) on compile
  • required: true, enum: and banner: on deploy
  • long_desc with \x5 line breaks on report
  • Sequential, parallel and mixed depends_on (spec, check, pipeline)
  • debug? and verbose? on status
  • sh with one line and with a heredoc (env_info, bootstrap)
  • A no_commands helper and a private helper
asgard                       # the default task, greet
asgard hello Alice
asgard compile --jobs 4 --tags debug release --defines VERSION:2 MODE:fast
asgard deploy --strategy rolling
asgard deploy                # Error: required option '--strategy' is missing
asgard help report           # the long_desc
asgard pipeline              # check → compile ∥ spec → pack → pipeline
asgard status --verbose --debug

See Defining Tasks, Options & Flags and Dependencies.

docs.title: server_subcommands.loki
docs.text:
A subcommand group, asgard server ..., in a class that inherits from Tasks:

  • ServerCommands < Tasks registered with subcommand "server", ServerCommands
  • Per-command options (--port, --daemon, --workers, --log, --force, --wait)
  • A helper (server_port) that reads the port saved by start so stop and restart use the same one
  • depends_on :stop inside the group, so restart stops first
asgard server                    # the group's own help
asgard server start -p 4000 --workers 4 --daemon
asgard server status
asgard server stop --force
asgard server restart            # stop → restart, on the saved port

See Subcommands.

docs.title: db_subcommands.loki
docs.text:
A second group, asgard db ..., with a longer dependency chain:

  • migrate [VERSION], rollback [STEPS], seed [FILE] with optional positional parameters
  • depends_on :rollback, :migrate, :seed on reset
  • long_desc and enum validation inside a subcommand class
asgard db migrate 20240101120000 --dry-run
asgard db rollback 3
asgard db seed --env staging
asgard db reset                  # rollback → migrate → seed → reset
asgard db console --env staging

docs.title: concurrent.loki
docs.text:
Proof that a parallel stage really runs at the same time. Three workers each print a letter ten times with random pauses; finish depends on all three.

depends_on :start, [:worker_a, :worker_b, :worker_c]
desc "Print end marker after all workers complete"
def finish = puts "\nfini - the end of concurrent task demo"

asgard finish

starting demo of concurrent task execution ...
ABCBACBACBABCBACBACBCABCABACBA
fini - the end of concurrent task demo

The letters interleave differently every run. The file sets $stdout.sync = true so each print appears at once. See Parallel Dependencies.

docs.title: do.loki
docs.text:
Asgard runs one task per command line. This example adds a do task that runs several, the way rake a b c or just a b c does. It is an ordinary user task, so you can copy it into any .loki:

require "shellwords"

class Tasks
  # Not a task (a class method), so it can be tested on its own:
  #   Tasks.do_steps("lint, hello Alice") #=> [["lint"], ["hello", "Alice"]]
  def self.do_steps(line)
    line.include?(",") ? line.split(",").map { |step| Shellwords.split(step) }.reject(&:empty?)
                       : Shellwords.split(line).map { |word| [word] }
  end

  desc "do STEPS...", "Run several tasks in sequence, e.g. `asgard do hello Alice, farewell Bob --formal`"
  stop_on_unknown_option! :do
  def do(*words)
    steps = self.class.do_steps(words.join(" "))
    raise Asgard::Error, "do: no tasks given" if steps.empty?

    steps.each do |name, *args|
      raise Asgard::Error, "do: unknown task '#{name}'" if name == "do" || !self.class.all_commands.key?(name)
      # Each step is parsed as if typed on its own command line.
      return :fail if self.class.send(:dispatch, nil, [name, *args], nil, shell: shell) == :fail
    end
  end
end

Steps are comma-separated so a step can carry its own arguments and options; with no commas, every word is a task.

asgard do greet finish
asgard do hello Alice, farewell Bob --formal, finish

Hello, Alice!
Goodbye, Bob.
...
  • Each step's arguments and options work exactly as they would alone.
  • The sequence stops at the first failure: a failing sh exits asgard, and a step that returns :fail makes do return :fail (exit 1).
  • Every task runs at most once per asgard invocation, so asgard do hello Alice, hello Bob greets only Alice, and a dependency shared by several steps runs once.

docs.title: confirm.loki
docs.text:
A guard: list confirm first in a dangerous task's depends_on and the task only runs after you answer yes. Also an ordinary user task, worth copying:

class Tasks
  # Not a task, so it can be tested on its own:
  #   Tasks.confirmed?("y", yes_env: nil) #=> true
  def self.confirmed?(answer, yes_env:)
    return true if yes_env && !yes_env.empty?

    %w[y yes].include?(answer.to_s.strip.downcase)
  end

  desc "Ask before running the task that depends on this", hide: true
  def confirm
    command = "asgard #{ARGV.join(' ')}"
    yes_env = env(:asgard_yes, "")
    return if self.class.confirmed?(nil, yes_env:)
    raise Asgard::Error, "refusing `#{command}`: no terminal to confirm on (set ASGARD_YES=1)" unless $stdin.tty?

    answer = ask("Really run `#{command}`? [y/N]")
    raise Asgard::Error, "aborted `#{command}`" unless self.class.confirmed?(answer, yes_env:)
  end

  depends_on :confirm
  desc "Pretend to drop and recreate the database (demo for confirm)"
  def reset_database
    puts "Database reset."
  end
end

asgard reset_database
# Really run `asgard reset_database`? [y/N] n
# asgard: aborted `asgard reset_database`          (exit 1)

ASGARD_YES=1 asgard reset_database                 # no question: scripts and CI
# Database reset.

Points the example makes:

  • Answering no raises Asgard::Error, which stops everything that has not run yet. Returning :fail would not: a dependency's return value never stops the task that depends on it.
  • A dependency does not know which task asked for it, so the question shows the whole command line.
  • With no terminal to ask on (a schedule, the watcher, a pipe) it refuses unless ASGARD_YES is set, rather than hanging.
  • hide: true keeps confirm out of asgard help.
  • It runs once per invocation, so asgard do reset_database, drop_cache asks once for the whole line. Keep it in its own first stage: in depends_on [:confirm, :backup], backup runs while the question waits.

ASGARD_YES is the example's own variable, not something asgard reads. See When a Dependency Fails.

docs.title: env_usage.loki and .env
docs.text:
Reading variables with env after loading a dotenv file:

class Tasks
  # loki_up finds .env in this directory or any ancestor, so the task
  # works from any subdirectory.
  dotenv loki_up(".env") || ".env"

  desc "Print environment variable values resolved via env()"
  def env_demo
    puts <<~OUT
      APP_NAME     : #{env(:app_name)}
      PORT         : #{env(:port)}
      API_KEY      : #{env(:api_key)}
      DATABASE_URL : #{env(:database_url)}
      LOG_LEVEL    : #{env(:log_level, "info")}
    OUT
  end
end

# examples/.env
APP_NAME=my_app
PORT=4000
API_KEY=secret-key-abc123
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/my_app_dev

asgard env_demo

APP_NAME     : my_app
PORT         : 4000
API_KEY      : secret-key-abc123
DATABASE_URL : postgres://localhost/my_app_dev
LOG_LEVEL    : info

LOG_LEVEL is not in .env, so env(:log_level, "info") returns the default. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: subdir/
docs.text:
Three files that show import across a directory boundary and import_up back out of one:

File What it does subdir/import_demo.loki Defines subdir_task; loaded by examples/.loki with import "subdir/import_demo.loki" subdir/.loki Makes subdir/ a project of its own when you run asgard from inside it; loads import_up_demo.loki subdir/import_up_demo.loki Calls import_up "env_usage.loki", which walks up and finds examples/env_usage.loki without a hard-coded relative path 
cd examples;        asgard subdir_task      # Loaded from examples/subdir/import_demo.loki
cd examples/subdir; asgard env_demo         # found one directory up by import_up

See Task Files.

docs.title: depends_on_block/good/ and depends_on_block/bad/
docs.text:
Two one-file projects for the block form of depends_on, which computes the dependency list after every file has loaded. Run each from its own directory.

good/.loki defines a_check, b_check, c_check and three tasks that gather them:

depends_on { [all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).sort.map(&:to_sym)] }
desc "Run every *_check task in parallel, then report"
def quality = puts "quality: all *_check tasks passed"

depends_on { [:setup, %i[a_check b_check], :teardown] }
desc "setup, then a_check+b_check in parallel, then teardown"
def full_cycle = puts "full_cycle: done"

depends_on do
  all_checks  = all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).sort.map(&:to_sym)
  slow_checks = %i[c_check]
  [:setup, all_checks - slow_checks, :teardown]
end
desc "setup, then every *_check except the slow ones, then teardown"
def smoke = puts "smoke: done"

cd examples/depends_on_block/good
asgard quality

running a_check ...
running b_check ...
running c_check ...
quality: all *_check tasks passed

bad/.loki wraps the list in one Array too many, [[ ... ]]. The result is checked before any task runs:

cd examples/depends_on_block/bad
asgard quality

asgard: depends_on proc/block for 'quality' returned invalid dependency [:a_check, :b_check, :c_check] (Array) in a parallel group; expected a Symbol or String

See Dynamic Dependencies.

docs.title: bad.loki
docs.text:
What goes wrong when parallel tasks share state through an instance variable, and why dep_result exists. Four workers run in one parallel stage and each adds to the same @hits counter a thousand times:

asgard bad_race

expected @hits == 4000, got 3127
DATA RACE CONFIRMED: 873 update(s) lost

Parallel dependencies each run on their own instance, so an instance variable is the wrong channel between them and the task that depends on them. Return the value from each task and read it with dep_result(:worker_1) instead. See Passing Results Between Tasks.

docs.title: watcher_examples/
docs.text:
A small project whose tasks run when its files change: four watch declarations covering a glob, a directory with only:, ignore: and env:, an events: filter with debounce:, and a second watch of one task with as:. The lib/, bin/, docs/ and data/ directories hold one placeholder file each so there is something to edit at once.

cd examples/watcher_examples
asgard watcher start
echo '# a change' >> lib/greeter.rb
asgard watcher log
asgard watcher list
asgard watcher stop

Every task also runs by hand, when changes is empty. Its README.md walks through the whole session with expected output; so does Watched Files.

docs.title: The asgard Repository Itself
docs.text: The repository root is a multi-file project that builds, tests and releases the gem. It is the best example of a .loki layout in real use.

docs.title: .loki
docs.text:
The entry point: imports, shared values, a header built from a helper, a watch, and a default_task.

import "quality.loki"
import "quality_rails.loki" if ENV["RAILS_ROOT"]   # a conditional import
import "gem_tasks.loki"
import "git.loki"
import "doc_tasks.loki"
import "xyzzy.loki"                                 # a deliberate override, for --doctor

class Tasks
  @@project      ||= "asgard".freeze
  @@project_desc ||= "CLI-task runner"

  watch :test_check, paths: %w[lib test], only: /\.rb\z/   # rerun the tests on save

  helper(:project_version) do
    @@project_version ||= File.read("lib/#{@@project}/version.rb").match(/VERSION\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/)[1].freeze
  end

  default_task :quality

  header <<~HEAD
    Project:  #{@@project} (v#{project_version}) - #{@@project_desc}
    Root Dir: #{loki_up.parent}
    Default task: #{default_task}
  HEAD
end

docs.title: quality.loki
docs.text:
The quality gates, and the convention that ties them together. Every gate is a task named *_check that writes its full output to <gate>_output.txt, prints one summary line, and returns a status: :pass, :fail, :warn (ran, non-blocking advice) or :skip (the tool is not installed). quality discovers every *_check task with a block depends_on, runs them all in parallel, reads each result with dep_result, and prints a summary table; it aborts only when a gate returned :fail.

desc "Run every *_check quality gate task in parallel"
depends_on -> { [all_commands.keys.grep(/_check\z/).sort.map(&:to_sym)] }
def quality
  check_tasks = self.class._deps.fetch(:quality, []).flatten.map(&:to_s)
  results = check_tasks.to_h { |name| [quality_gate_label(name), dep_result(name)] }
  print_quality_summary(results)
end

Because a *_check task returns :fail rather than exiting, every gate runs to the end and the summary shows all failures at once. Run alone (asgard rubocop_check), a gate that returns :fail still makes asgard exit 1.

asgard quality

Tests: 412 runs, 1193 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips (see test_output.txt)
RuboCop: 61 files inspected, no offenses detected (see rubocop_output.txt)
...
============================================================
Quality Gate Summary
============================================================
  [PASS] Tests + Coverage
  [PASS] RuboCop
  [SKIP] Typos
  ...
------------------------------------------------------------
  9 pass, 1 skip
============================================================

All quality gates passed.

docs.title: gem_tasks.loki
docs.text: console, build (depends on quality), install (depends on build) and release (depends on quality, asks for confirmation unless --yes, refuses a dirty working tree or an existing tag). A plain sh sequence does the work; project_version comes from the helper in .loki.

docs.title: git.loki
docs.text: Three one-liners: push, pull (fast-forward only), fetch. The smallest useful task file.

docs.title: doc_tasks.loki
docs.text:
Tasks that only exist when the project has the matching tool, decided with ordinary Ruby if around the defs. The documentation server is a background job:

class Tasks
  root = loki_up.dirname

  if root.join("mkdocs.yml").exist?
    desc "Documentation builder"
    def doc_builder = sh "mkdocs build"

    desc "Documentation server, as a background job (see `asgard jobs`)"
    depends_on :doc_builder
    def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve", background: true
  end
end

asgard doc_server        # started doc_server-1 (pid 48213), log: ...
asgard jobs              # lists it
asgard jobs stop doc_server

See Background Jobs.

docs.title: xyzzy.loki
docs.text:
Defines a xyzzy task; .loki, loaded after it, defines xyzzy again. The first definition is silently dead, and asgard --doctor says so:

  .loki
    xyzzy  .loki:26   active — redefines xyzzy.loki:6

  xyzzy.loki
    xyzzy  xyzzy.loki:6   OVERRIDDEN by .loki:26 — never callable

See Help & Diagnostics.

docs.title: quality_rails.loki
docs.text: Rails-only gates (brakeman_check, rails_best_practices_check, active_record_doctor_check), imported by .loki only when RAILS_ROOT is set. Nothing else needs to change for quality to pick them up: its block depends_on finds every *_check task that is loaded.

docs.title: Files & Directories
docs.text: Everything asgard reads from and writes to disk: the files in your project, the per-project state it keeps outside the repository, the job files it hands to the system scheduler, and the temporary files a script runs from. Use this page when you want to know where something went, what is safe to delete, and what to back up.

docs.title: In Your Project
docs.text:
File Who writes it Purpose .loki you The project root marker and entry point. Asgard walks up from the current directory and loads the first .loki it finds. It may be empty. *.loki you More task files, loaded only when .loki calls import. .env (or any name) you Variables loaded by a dotenv call in a .loki. Never loaded unless asked. .envrc you A direnv file. Scheduled and watched tasks run under direnv exec when direnv is on PATH, so these variables reach them at run time.

Asgard writes nothing into the project directory itself. See Task Files and Environment Variables.

docs.title: The Project Slug
docs.text:
Every project's state is filed under a slug: the name of the directory holding .loki, a dash, and eight hex digits derived from the directory's full real path.

api-9f3a1c2b
watcher-examples-5e1d0c3a

The hash is what keeps two projects in directories of the same name apart: two checkouts called api, a repository and a fork beside it, two examples/ directories. It is stable for as long as the project stays where it is, and it is the same whether you reach the project through a symlink or its real path.

To find a project's slug:

asgard schedule list --all    # Project: api-9f3a1c2b (/Users/you/work/api)
asgard watcher list --all
asgard jobs list --all
asgard watcher start          # started watcher for api-9f3a1c2b (pid 123); log: ...

Moving or renaming the project changes the slug. Its old schedules, watcher state and job records are then listed under the old slug as another project, flagged [root missing]; see Scheduled Tasks and asgard schedule prune in the Command Reference.

docs.title: Per-Project State
docs.text:
Watcher state and background job records live under one state directory:

$XDG_STATE_HOME/asgard/          # default: ~/.local/state/asgard/
  watch/<slug>/
  jobs/<slug>/

Each <slug> directory is created readable by its owner only (mode 0700), because logs and job scripts can hold secrets. Each holds a root file naming the project directory, which is how the list --all commands find every project without loading its .loki.

docs.title: watch/<slug>/
docs.text:
File Contents watcher.pid The pid of the running watcher watcher.lock A lock the running watcher holds, so a second watcher start is refused watcher.log One line per trigger, spawn and exit, plus every triggered task's output watcher.log.1 The previous log, once watcher.log grew past the limit (see Log Rotation) declarations.json The watch declarations recorded at start, which list --all shows for other projects entries/<name>.json One record per entry with its last run: pid, status, duration, finish time changes/<name>-<n>.json A change list too large for the environment, handed to the task through ASGARD_CHANGES_FILE root The project directory

See Watched Files.

docs.title: jobs/<slug>/
docs.text:
File Contents <name>.json The job's record: name, owning task, pid, start time, working directory, script path, log path, first script line <name>.sh The script exactly as handed to the shell; the extension is the shell's (.py for :python3, and so on) <name>.log stdout and stderr of the job's latest run; emptied on each new start of that name <name>.status The exit status, written when the job ends root The project directory

A job's files stay until the next start of the same name or asgard jobs clean, so the log of a crashed job can still be read. See Background Jobs.

docs.title: Scheduler Files
docs.text:
asgard schedule install writes one job per declared entry into the system scheduler's own directory. The files are written readable by their owner only (mode 0600), since they carry the declaration's env: values.

macOS (launchd)Linux (systemd) What Where Job definition ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.madbomber.asgard.<slug>.<name>.plist Log ~/Library/Logs/asgard/com.madbomber.asgard.<slug>.<name>.log

asgard schedule preview prints the plist before anything is installed. A stopped entry is recorded by launchd itself (launchctl print-disabled), not in a file of asgard's.

What Where Service unit $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user/asgard.<slug>.<name>.service (default ~/.config/systemd/user/) Timer unit $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user/asgard.<slug>.<name>.timer Log $XDG_STATE_HOME/asgard/asgard.<slug>.<name>.log (default ~/.local/state/asgard/)

asgard schedule preview prints both units. Needs systemd 240 or later.

asgard schedule list ends with the log directory and the command that reads a log: Logs: <dir> (asgard schedule log NAME). See Scheduled Tasks.

docs.title: Temporary Files
docs.text:
Every sh and shebang call writes its script to a file in the system temporary directory, named like asgard_20261024-80545-bmbloc.sh with the shell's extension, runs the shell on that file, and deletes it when the script ends. Two things follow:

  • $0 inside a script is that temporary path, not bash or a command name. Print a name you choose in usage messages.
  • Nothing accumulates. There is nothing to clean up after a foreground script, even one that failed.

A background job's script is not temporary: it is kept as jobs/<slug>/<name>.sh so that asgard jobs can verify the job is still the process it started. See Shell Commands.

docs.title: Log Rotation
docs.text:
watcher.log is moved to watcher.log.1 (replacing any older .1) once it is larger than 10 MB, and a fresh watcher.log starts. Set ASGARD_LOG_MAX to a number of bytes to change the limit:

ASGARD_LOG_MAX=1048576 asgard watcher start    # rotate at 1 MB

Job logs are not rotated; each new start of a job name empties its log. Scheduler logs are appended by launchd or systemd and are not rotated by asgard.

docs.title: What Is Safe to Delete
docs.text:
Delete by hand Safe? Use instead jobs/<slug>/ files of a job that is not running yes, but asgard jobs clean removes exactly those watch/<slug>/watcher.log, watcher.log.1 yes a running watcher starts a fresh log on its next line watch/<slug>/entries/*.json yes list then shows never for those entries watch/<slug>/ of a project whose watcher is stopped yes watch/<slug>/watcher.pid or watcher.lock of a running watcher no asgard watcher stop; the watcher cannot be stopped or restarted cleanly without them jobs/<slug>/<name>.json of a running job no asgard jobs stop NAME; without the record the job cannot be listed or stopped and must be found with ps A plist or systemd unit no asgard schedule remove NAME, which also unloads the job from the scheduler The whole ~/.local/state/asgard/ only with every watcher stopped and every job stopped

The supported ways to tidy up are asgard jobs clean, asgard schedule remove, asgard schedule prune and asgard watcher stop. See the Command Reference.

docs.title: Environment Variables That Change Paths
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect XDG_STATE_HOME ~/.local/state Base of the state directory (<base>/asgard/) and, on Linux, the scheduler logs XDG_CONFIG_HOME ~/.config Base of the systemd user unit directory (Linux) ASGARD_LOG_MAX 10485760 Bytes before watcher.log rotates

The full list of variables asgard reads and sets is in Environment Variables.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page takes you from nothing to a working project in a few minutes: install asgard, create a .loki file, define a task, run it, and add a parameter and an option. Each step is a complete, runnable example. The last section shows how a project grows past one file.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
RubyGemsBundler 
gem install asgard

This installs the asgard command for your Ruby. The gem compiles one native extension, so a C++17 compiler must be present (Xcode's command-line tools on macOS, build-essential or the equivalent on Linux).

To pin the version a project uses, add it to the project's Gemfile:

bundle add asgard

Then run it through Bundler so the pinned version is the one that runs:

bundle exec asgard hello

The rest of this manual writes plain asgard ...; prefix bundle exec if you installed it this way.

Check the installation:

asgard --version

0.6.0

--version works anywhere, even in a directory with no project.

docs.title: Create Your First Task File
docs.text:
Every project has one file named .loki at its root. It does two jobs: it marks the project root, so you can run asgard from any subdirectory, and it holds (or loads) your tasks.

cd ~/work/myproject
touch .loki

Open .loki in your editor and add a task:

class Tasks
  desc "Say hello to the world"
  def hello = puts "Hello, World!"
end

Note

Tasks already exists when your file loads; asgard defines it. You reopen the class and add methods. There is nothing to require and no superclass to name.

docs.title: Run Your Task
docs.text:
asgard hello

Hello, World!

See every task the project defines:

asgard help

asgard v0.6.0 The Mighty Thor and Loki working for you

Commands:
  asgard hello                # Say hello to the world
  asgard help [COMMAND]       # Describe available commands or one specific command
  asgard jobs SUBCOMMAND      # List, stop and restart the background jobs started with `sh ..., background: true`
  asgard schedule SUBCOMMAND  # Manage schedules declared with `schedule :task, ...` (launchd on macOS, systemd on Linux)
  asgard tree                 # Print a tree of all available commands
  asgard watcher SUBCOMMAND   # Run and manage the file watcher declared with `watch :task, paths: ...`

Options:
  [--debug]    # Enable debug mode ($DEBUG = true)
  [--verbose]  # Enable verbose output ($VERBOSE = true)
  [--version]  # Show asgard version and exit
  [--doctor]   # Diagnose .loki resolution, imports, and task definitions for the CWD, then exit

Documentation ... https://madbomber.github.io/asgard
Github Repo ..... https://github.com/MadBomber/asgard

Your hello sits beside asgard's built-in commands: help, tree, and the three management commands schedule, watcher and jobs, which have their own pages later in this manual.

Help for one task:

asgard help hello

Usage:
  asgard hello

Options:
  [--debug]    # Enable debug mode ($DEBUG = true)
  ...

Say hello to the world

docs.title: Add a Parameter
docs.text:
A positional parameter is a parameter of the method. Give it a default so the task also runs with nothing after its name, and name it in the first argument of desc so the help shows it:

class Tasks
  desc "greet NAME", "Greet someone by name"
  def greet(name = "World")
    puts "Hello, #{name}!"
  end
end

asgard greet
asgard greet Alice

Hello, World!
Hello, Alice!

Without a default, the parameter is required and asgard greet prints a usage error and exits 1.

docs.title: Add an Option
docs.text:
option declares a named flag for the task that follows it. Inside the task, a boolean reads as options.name?; any option's value is options.name or options[:name]:

class Tasks
  desc "greet NAME", "Greet someone by name"
  option :shout, aliases: "-s", type: :boolean, desc: "Uppercase the greeting"
  def greet(name = "World")
    message = "Hello, #{name}!"
    puts options.shout? ? message.upcase : message
  end
end

asgard greet Alice --shout
asgard greet Alice -s

HELLO, ALICE!
HELLO, ALICE!

asgard help greet now lists --shout with its description. Options can be strings, numbers, lists and more; see Defining Tasks.

docs.title: Type Less
docs.text:
Any unambiguous prefix of a task name runs it:

asgard gre          # same as: asgard greet
asgard hel Bob      # Ambiguous command hel matches [hello, help]
asgard hello        # an exact name always wins

When a prefix matches more than one task, asgard lists the candidates instead of guessing. map gives a task a short name that stays stable; see Command Aliases.

docs.title: Run a Shell Command
docs.text:
Most tasks run programs. sh runs a command, or a whole script, under the default shell (bash unless the project picks another) and prints it first:

class Tasks
  desc "Show the Ruby version"
  def ruby_version = sh "ruby --version"

  desc "Install dependencies and run the tests"
  def check
    sh <<~SHELL
      bundle install --quiet
      bundle exec rake test
    SHELL
  end
end

asgard ruby_version

ruby --version
ruby 3.4.1 (2024-12-25 revision 48d4efcb85) +PRISM [arm64-darwin24]

When a command fails, asgard stops there and exits with the command's status, so a pipeline never silently continues past a broken step:

asgard check; echo "exit: $?"

bundle install --quiet
bundle exec rake test
...
rake aborted!
exit: 1

Ruby's own ways of running a program, system, backticks and the rest, work in a task too. sh and its sibling shebang add what a task runner needs around the command: the echo, the stop on failure with the right exit status, a pinned shell so the script behaves the same under the watcher and a schedule, and background: true for a process that outlives asgard. The comparison is in sh Versus Ruby's Own Methods; Python, Node and other interpreters, and how to pick which bash runs, are on the same Shell Commands page.

docs.title: Built-in Flags
docs.text:
Every task accepts four flags that belong to asgard itself:

Flag What it does --version Print asgard's version and exit, before any task file loads --doctor Print a diagnosis of the project's .loki files (what loaded, what each file defines, overridden tasks, dependency problems) and exit --debug Set $DEBUG before the task runs; debug? returns true inside the task --verbose Set $VERBOSE before the task runs; verbose? returns true inside the task 
asgard --version
asgard --doctor
asgard greet --debug
asgard greet --verbose Alice

Note

--version and --doctor are asgard's own flags only when they come before the task name. After it, they belong to the task: asgard greet --version passes --version to greet.

Inside a task, debug? and verbose? let you add detail on request:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build
    puts "building with #{options.inspect}" if debug?
    sh verbose? ? "rake build --trace" : "rake build"
  end
end

The --doctor report is explained on Help & Diagnostics.

docs.title: Growing the Project
docs.text:
One .loki is enough for a while. When it gets long, split tasks by concern into sibling files and have .loki load them:

myproject/
  .loki          ← root marker; loads the others
  build.loki     ← build tasks
  deploy.loki    ← deploy tasks
  qa.loki        ← test and lint tasks

# .loki
import "*.loki"

class Tasks
  @@app ||= "myproject".freeze
end

# qa.loki
class Tasks
  desc "Run the tests"
  def test = sh "bundle exec rake test"
end

Each *.loki file reopens the same Tasks class, so tasks in one file can depend on tasks in another, and a value set in .loki is visible everywhere. import "*.loki" loads the siblings in alphabetical order; import "deploy.loki" loads one by name. The rules are on Task Files.
