docs.title: Helper Methods
docs.text:
Not every method in a .loki is a task. A method that computes a version string, wraps a repeated sh call or formats output is a helper: something tasks call, that nobody types on the command line. Asgard gives you three ways to write one, and this page says which to use when.

The simplest and most common is private:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile and package"
  def build
    compile("src")
    package(app_version)
  end

  private

  def compile(dir)     = sh "gcc -O2 -o bin/myapp #{dir}/*.c"
  def package(ver)     = sh "tar czf pkg/myapp-#{ver}.tar.gz bin/"
  def app_version      = `git describe --tags`.strip
end

asgard build        # runs compile, then package
asgard compile      # Could not find command "compile".

A public method without a desc is a task

A public def with no desc above it is a hidden task: it does not appear in asgard help, but asgard name runs it and depends_on :name accepts it. A helper must therefore be private, sit inside a no_commands block, or be defined with helper. asgard --doctor lists hidden tasks, which is a quick way to find a helper that was left public by mistake.

docs.title: Private Methods
docs.text:
Everything after private in a class body is a private method: callable from any task in the same class, invisible to the command line and to asgard help:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile and package"
  def build
    compile("src")
    package(app_version)
  end

  desc "Build and publish to RubyGems"
  def release
    build
    sh "gem push pkg/myapp-#{app_version}.gem"
  end

  private

  def compile(dir)
    sh "gcc -O2 -o bin/myapp #{dir}/*.c"
  end

  def package(ver)
    sh "tar czf pkg/myapp-#{ver}.tar.gz bin/"
  end

  def app_version
    `git describe --tags`.strip
  end
end

private applies to every method defined after it in that class body, so the usual layout is tasks first, one private, then the helpers. A .loki that reopens Tasks later starts public again.

A helper can use everything a task can: sh and shebang, options, env, changes, dep_result, and the @@ variables.

docs.title: The no_commands Block
docs.text:
no_commands do ... end marks the methods inside it as not being tasks, while leaving them public. Use it when a helper must stay public, for instance so a subcommand class or an included module can call it from outside:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build
    puts "Revision: #{current_sha}"
    sh "rake build"
  end

  no_commands do
    def current_sha = `git rev-parse --short HEAD`.strip
    def timestamp   = Time.now.strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
  end
end

A no_commands block may sit anywhere in the class body, including between a desc and the task it describes; the desc still attaches to the task.

docs.title: The helper DSL Method
docs.text:
Some values are needed in two places: inside task bodies, and in the class body itself, where header, footer and @@ initializers run. A plain def only makes a method for task bodies; a def self.name only makes one for the class body. helper defines both from one block:

class Tasks
  @@project ||= "myapp".freeze

  helper(:version) {
    @@version ||= File.read("lib/myapp/version.rb")[/VERSION\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/, 1].freeze
  }

  header "#{@@project} v#{version}"     # class body: used while the file loads

  desc "Show version"
  def show_version = puts version       # task body: used when the task runs
end

asgard help | head -3
# myapp v1.4.0
# ...
asgard show_version
# 1.4.0

Without helper, the same thing takes two definitions:

def self.version = File.read("lib/myapp/version.rb")[/VERSION\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/, 1].freeze
no_commands { private def version = self.class.version }

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
The block takes any signature a Ruby method can: positional, keyword, defaults, a block:

helper(:project_root) { loki_up.dirname.to_s }
helper(:gem_path)     { |name| "lib/#{name}/version.rb" }
helper(:tag_prefix)   { |sep = "-"| "#{@@project}#{sep}" }
helper(:format_version) { |name, version, prefix: "v", separator: "-"|
  "#{prefix}#{name}#{separator}#{version}"
}

A wrong number of arguments or an unknown keyword raises the ordinary Ruby ArgumentError.

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: A helper method never appears in asgard help, cannot be run from the command line, and is private inside task bodies.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text: Use helper when a value is needed both while the file loads (a header, a @@ default) and while a task runs. For a helper that only task bodies call, private is simpler.

docs.title: Choosing Between Them
docs.text:
private no_commands helper Hidden from asgard help Yes Yes Yes Runnable from the command line No No No Usable in task bodies Yes Yes Yes Usable in the class body (header, @@ defaults) No No Yes Callable from outside the class (a module, a subclass's class body) No Yes Class side only Looks like Plain Ruby Thor Asgard

For most helpers, private. Use no_commands when the method must stay public, and helper when the class body needs it too.

docs.title: A Ruby Module in the Project
docs.text:
Put shared helpers in a plain Ruby file as a module, load it with require_relative, and include it in Tasks. Methods declared private inside the module stay private, so they are helpers, not tasks:

# shared/helpers.rb
module BuildHelpers
  private

  def compile(dir)
    sh "gcc -O2 -o bin/myapp #{dir}/*.c"
  end

  def dist_path(ver)
    "pkg/myapp-#{ver}.tar.gz"
  end
end

# .loki
require_relative "shared/helpers"

class Tasks
  include BuildHelpers

  desc "Compile the project"
  def build = compile("src")

  desc "Create distribution archive"
  def package = sh "tar czf #{dist_path(app_version)} bin/"
end

Tip

A module method runs as part of the task, so it can call sh, shebang, env, changes, options and dep_result exactly as a method written in Tasks can.

docs.title: A Shared .loki Up the Tree
docs.text:
When several projects share a set of tasks (not just helpers), keep them in a .loki file in a common ancestor directory and load it with import_up, which finds the file without knowing how deep the project sits:

~/sandbox/
  shared_tasks.loki     ← tasks every project gets
  projectA/
    .loki               ← import_up "shared_tasks.loki"
  projectB/
    .loki               ← import_up "shared_tasks.loki"

# projectA/.loki
import_up "shared_tasks.loki"

class Tasks
  # the shared tasks and helpers are defined by here
end

import_up returns false instead of failing when the file is not found, so it is safe in a project that may or may not have the shared file above it. See Task Files for import, import_up and loki_up.

docs.title: Helpers in Subcommands
docs.text:
A subcommand class inherits from Tasks, so it inherits every private helper, no_commands method and helper defined there. It can also define its own:

class DeployCommands < Tasks
  desc "Deploy to staging"
  def staging = deploy_to("staging")

  desc "Deploy to production"
  def production = deploy_to("production")

  private

  def deploy_to(env)
    sh "cap #{env} deploy REV=#{current_sha}"   # current_sha comes from Tasks
  end
end

class Tasks
  desc "deploy SUBCOMMAND", "Deploy the application"
  subcommand "deploy", DeployCommands
end

See Subcommands.

docs.title: Names to Avoid
docs.text: A helper cannot take a name that asgard or Thor use internally: shell, options, invoke, run, args and a few others. A .loki that defines one, as a task or as a helper, is refused when it loads, with the file and line. The list is in Defining Tasks.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
A task can start a process that keeps running after the task, and after asgard itself, has finished: a documentation server, a database, an API under development. sh "mkdocs serve", background: true starts one as a job, and the built-in asgard jobs command lists, stops, restarts and cleans up every job the project has started.

Jobs are built in. There is nothing to install or require, and a job's shell comes from the same shells registry a foreground script uses.

docs.title: The Shortest Example
docs.text:
# .loki
class Tasks
  desc "Serve the documentation"
  def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve", background: true
end

asgard doc_server

mkdocs serve
started doc_server-1 (pid 48213), log: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/jobs/api-9f3a1c2b/doc_server-1.log

The prompt comes straight back; the server is running. Later, from any directory in the project:

asgard jobs

┌──────────────┬────────────┬───────┬─────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ JOB          │ TASK       │ PID   │ STATUS  │ STARTED             │ COMMAND      │
├──────────────┼────────────┼───────┼─────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────┤
│ doc_server-1 │ doc_server │ 48213 │ running │ 2026-10-24 09:30:01 │ mkdocs serve │
└──────────────┴────────────┴───────┴─────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────┘

State: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/jobs

asgard jobs log doc_server-1        # what it has printed so far
asgard jobs stop doc_server-1       # stopped doc_server-1 (pid 48213)

docs.title: Three Ways a Script Runs
docs.text:
sh and shebang run a script in one of three modes. The first two are asgard's; the third is the shell's, and it is worth knowing what you give up when you use it.

The three ways a script runs: in the foreground asgard waits for the exit status; as a managed background job asgard records the job and returns at once; detached with an ampersand the shell exits and asgard knows nothing about the process.

Foreground sh "rake build" the task waits here bash runs the script output in your terminal start exit status non-zero: asgard exits with it zero: the next statement runs

Managed background sh "mkdocs serve", background: true returns a job object at once job: doc_server-1 own session, name, pid, log recorded asgard jobs list, log, stop, restart, later outlives asgard

Detached sh "mkdocs serve &" reports success at once bash exits immediately the & hands the process off process floats free asgard knows nothing about it

Foreground: asgard waits. Managed background: asgard records the job and can find it again. Detached: the shell hands the process off and asgard never hears of it. Mode How you ask for it The task When asgard exits asgard jobs Foreground sh "rake build" Waits for the script to finish before its next statement; a failure exits asgard with the script's status The script has already finished Nothing to manage Managed background sh "mkdocs serve", background: true Continues at once with a job object in hand The job keeps running Lists, stops, restarts and cleans it Detached sh "mkdocs serve &" (or nohup, setsid, disown inside the script) Continues at once with true; the shell has already exited The process keeps running Knows nothing about it

docs.title: Foreground
docs.text:
The default. The script runs under the default shell, asgard waits for it, and the task moves on only when it has finished. A non-zero exit ends the asgard process with that status, so a failed step stops the pipeline. See Shell Commands.

def build
  sh "rake build"        # the task waits here
  sh "rake test"         # and only then runs this
end

docs.title: Managed Background
docs.text:
background: true (or background: :name) starts the script as a job. The call returns at once with a job object, the task continues with its next statement, and the job runs on in its own session with its output in a log file. When asgard exits the job is still running, and it is still asgard's: its pid, log and owning task are recorded on disk, so a later asgard jobs list shows it, asgard jobs stop ends it, and asgard jobs restart runs its task again.

def servers
  sh "docker compose up postgres", background: true   # servers-1
  sh "bin/rails server",            background: :api  # api
  puts "both up; see `asgard jobs list`"               # runs immediately
end

docs.title: Detached
docs.text:
A trailing &, or nohup, setsid or disown inside the script, hands the process to the shell's own background handling. It runs in the background much like a managed job, with two differences that matter:

  • No management data is saved. The shell exits without waiting, asgard sees that clean exit and reports the step as a success, and nothing records the pid, the log or the task. asgard jobs cannot list, stop, restart or clean it. Running the task again starts a second copy. An error after the &, even a misspelled command, is invisible to asgard.
  • It is detached from asgard completely. The process is reparented to the system when asgard exits, and you manage it some other way: ps, pgrep, kill, or whatever the program itself offers. Unless the script redirects them, its stdout and stderr are still your terminal, so its output keeps landing on top of your prompt after asgard has returned, and Ctrl-C at that prompt no longer reaches it.

Detaching is the right tool when you really do want a process asgard should never touch. For anything you expect to come back to, use background:.

# Detached: asgard reports success and forgets it exists.
def docs_detached = sh "nohup mkdocs serve > mkdocs.log 2>&1 &"

# Managed: listed, logged, stoppable, restartable.
def docs = sh "mkdocs serve", background: true

docs.title: Starting a Job
docs.text:
sh and shebang both take background::

class Tasks
  desc "Serve the documentation"
  def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve", background: true

  desc "Bring up the development stack"
  depends_on :db
  def servers
    sh "bin/rails server", background: :api
    shebang :python3, "import http.server; http.server.test()", background: :static
  end

  desc "Start the database"
  def db = sh "postgres -D tmp/db", background: true
end
background: Job name Notes nil or false none Foreground; the default true <task>-<N> Named after the task whose body made the call, plus a counter: doc_server-1, servers-1, servers-2. Must be called from inside a task a Symbol or String the name itself Letters, digits and _ only; never looks like an automatic name anything else ArgumentError

The counter restarts at 1 each time a task body runs, so re-running servers while servers-1 is still up names the second call servers-2 again, and a dependency running in a parallel stage names its jobs after itself (db-1), not after the task you typed. Named jobs never consume a number: true, :api, true yields servers-1, api, servers-2, so adding or removing a named job never renumbers the rest. Job names are unique per project across tasks; two tasks that both say background: :server share one slot.

The call echoes the script as usual, then prints one line and returns:

mkdocs serve
started doc_server-1 (pid 48213), log: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/jobs/api-9f3a1c2b/doc_server-1.log

The return value is a job object with name, task, pid and log, in case the task wants to print or wait on something. silent: true suppresses both the echo and the started line.

docs.title: Already Running
docs.text: Starting a job whose name is already running starts nothing. The call prints doc_server-1 already running (pid 48213, started by doc_server), log: <path> and returns the existing job. A job whose record is on disk but whose process is gone is replaced: the old record, script and status are removed, the log is emptied, and the new process starts.

docs.title: Failure
docs.text: A missing shell exits 127 up front, as foreground sh does, because nothing would otherwise be watching for it. Every other failure happens after the call has returned and shows up in the listing as an exit status, and in the log. There is no automatic rollback; jobs already started by the same task body stay up.

docs.title: The Job's Environment
docs.text: The job inherits the task's environment plus ASGARD_JOB (its name) and ASGARD_JOB_STATUS (the file its exit status is written to). PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 is set unless you set it yourself, because Python fully buffers stdout when it is a file and a print loop would otherwise show nothing in the log until exit. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Managing Jobs
docs.text:
asgard jobs                   # same as list
asgard jobs list              # this project's jobs: running, exited with a status, or gone
asgard jobs list --all        # every project's, grouped by project
asgard jobs stop              # stop every job of this project
asgard jobs stop api          # stop one job by name
asgard jobs stop servers      # stop every job started by a task, and by the tasks it depends on
asgard jobs stop --all        # stop every project's jobs
asgard jobs stop api -t 30    # wait 30s after TERM before KILL (default 10)
asgard jobs log api           # print the log
asgard jobs log api -f        # follow it (tail -f)
asgard jobs restart api       # stop it, then run its owning task again
asgard jobs clean             # forget every job that is no longer running

docs.title: list
docs.text:
One row per job with its name, owning task, pid, status, start time and the first line of its script:

┌──────────────┬────────────┬───────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────┐
│ JOB          │ TASK       │ PID   │ STATUS          │ STARTED             │ COMMAND       │
├──────────────┼────────────┼───────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────────┼───────────────┤
│ db-1         │ db         │ 48201 │ running         │ 2026-10-24 09:30:01 │ postgres -D … │
│ api          │ servers    │ 48213 │ exited 1 (2.5s) │ 2026-10-24 09:30:02 │ bin/rails se… │
│ doc_server-1 │ doc_server │ 47990 │ gone            │ 2026-10-23 17:12:40 │ mkdocs serve  │
└──────────────┴────────────┴───────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────────┴───────────────┘

State: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/jobs
Status Meaning running The recorded pid is alive and is still the process asgard started exited N (Ns) The job ended with status N after that long; 143 is a TERM, 137 a KILL gone Neither: the process is not there and no status was written. The machine rebooted, or something killed the job outright

Run from a directory with no .loki above it, list covers every project, as --all does. With no jobs recorded:

No jobs recorded for api-9f3a1c2b. Start one with `sh "...", background: true` inside a task.
Use `asgard jobs list --all` to see every project's jobs.

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
Each name is first tried as a job name, then as a task name: stop servers ends every job that servers started and, through depends_on, every job its dependencies started (db-1). Resolving a task name reads the project's .loki, so that form works inside the project. No name stops every job of the project; --all stops every project's. Jobs stop newest first.

Each job gets TERM to its whole process group, so the shell and everything it started go together. After a second of waiting the command says so, and when the grace period runs out (--timeout, default 10 seconds) it sends KILL and waits until the pid is gone. One line per job:

stopped api (pid 48213)
waiting for db-1 (pid 48201)
killed db-1 (pid 48201) after 10s
doc_server-1 is not running

The exit status is 1 when any job had to be killed or any name matched nothing (jobs: no such job or task: apii). Records stay, so the log of a stopped job can still be read; clean removes them.

docs.title: log
docs.text: Prints the job's log, stdout and stderr together, from its latest start (each start empties it). -f follows it as tail -f does. A job that has not written yet still has an empty log.

docs.title: restart
docs.text: Stops the job, then runs its owning task again in the same asgard process, dependencies included. A job started with a chosen name from outside a task body has no owning task and cannot be restarted: jobs: static was not started from a task, so there is nothing to run again.

docs.title: clean
docs.text: Removes the record, script, status and log of every job that is not verified running, and prints removed NAME for each. Nothing that is running is touched. With nothing to do: Nothing to clean for api-9f3a1c2b.

docs.title: How a Job Runs
docs.text:
A job starts in a new session of its own: it has no controlling terminal, so closing the terminal that started it does not reach it, and it leads its own process group, which is what stop signals as a whole so the shell and everything it started go together.

The recorded pid belongs to a small /bin/sh wrapper that runs your script's shell as its child, waits for it, and writes the exit status to a status file when it ends. That is how list can show exited 1 (2.5s) for a job nobody was waiting on. The wrapper is always /bin/sh, whatever your default_shell is; your script still runs under the shell you asked for. Because the recorded pid is the wrapper, an exec inside your script replaces only the inner shell and the job stays verifiable.

The job's stdin is /dev/null, so it can never stop waiting for keyboard input, and its stdout and stderr are appended to the log.

A job is verified, not assumed, every time asgard looks at it: the pid must be alive and its command line must still carry the job's script path. A pid reused by an unrelated process after a reboot fails that check and the job shows as gone rather than as somebody else's process.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Everything lives under ~/.local/state/asgard/jobs/<slug>/ (or $XDG_STATE_HOME/asgard/jobs/<slug>/), where the slug is the project directory's name plus a short hash of its full path, the same slug schedules and watchers use:

File Contents <name>.json The record: name, task, pid, start time, working directory, script path, log path, first script line <name>.sh (or the shell's extension) The script exactly as handed to the shell <name>.log stdout and stderr of the latest run <name>.status The exit status, written when the job ends root The project root, so list --all can find every project without loading its .loki

The directory is readable by you alone, since logs and scripts can hold secrets. A job's files stay until the next start of that name or asgard jobs clean, so the log of a crashed job can still be read. A new start of the same name removes the old record, script and status and empties the log; clean deletes all four.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
A development stack. Give each server a name, put the database in a dependency, and one command brings everything up:

class Tasks
  desc "Start the database"
  def db = sh "postgres -D tmp/db", background: :db

  desc "Bring up the whole development stack"
  depends_on :db
  def servers
    sh "bin/rails server -p 3000", background: :api
    sh "bin/vite dev",             background: :assets
    sh "mkdocs serve",             background: :docs
  end
end

asgard servers            # db, api, assets, docs
asgard jobs               # all four, running
asgard jobs stop servers  # all four, including db, because servers depends on db
asgard jobs restart api   # just the API, by running servers again (db is already up, so it is reused)

A one-word stop. asgard jobs stop servers is the normal way down. A task may wrap it when you want a name of your own:

desc "Stop the development stack"
def down = sh "asgard jobs stop servers"

Jobs from watchers and schedules. A task run by the watcher or by a schedule may start jobs. They are recorded under the project's slug like any other, so asgard jobs from the project directory shows them as if you had started them by hand.

docs.title: Jobs, Watchers and Schedules
docs.text:
The three built-ins answer different questions:

  • A job is a process a task starts on purpose, by name, that outlives asgard. It is not a supervisor: a job that crashes stays down and shows as exited until you restart it.
  • A watcher runs tasks when files change.
  • A schedule runs tasks on a timer.

They compose. A task run by the watcher or by a schedule may start jobs; the records are on disk under the project's slug, so they are visible to asgard jobs from the project directory.

docs.title: Name Collisions
docs.text: The built-in command is registered under a reserved name and mapped to jobs. If your .loki defines its own task called jobs, asgard jobs still runs the built-in; name your task something else.

docs.title: Options & Flags
docs.text: Options are the --name value and --flag words after a task name. A task declares its own with option; a class declares options that every task accepts with class_option; and asgard adds four flags of its own to every task: --version, --doctor, --debug and --verbose. This page covers all three layers, where options[...] can be read, and the reference tables for option types and keys.

docs.title: Per-Task Options
docs.text:
option (the long name is method_option) declares a flag for the task that follows it. The value is in options[:name] inside the task:

class Tasks
  desc "deploy ENV", "Deploy to ENV"
  option :branch,  aliases: "-b", type: :string,  default: "main", desc: "Git branch to deploy"
  option :dry_run, aliases: "-n", type: :boolean, default: false,  desc: "Print commands without running them"
  def deploy(env = "staging")
    if options.dry_run?
      puts "Would deploy #{options.branch} to #{env}"
    else
      sh "cap #{env} deploy BRANCH=#{options.branch}"
    end
  end
end

asgard deploy production -b release --dry-run

Would deploy release to production

options is a hash with symbol keys that also answers method calls: options.branch is options[:branch], and a boolean reads as a predicate, options.dry_run?, which is always true or false. An option that was not given and has no default is nil, so options[:tags] is nil rather than an empty array. Both --branch release and --branch=release work; a multi-word option name is typed with a dash, --dry-run, and read with an underscore, options[:dry_run].

The full set of types and keys is on Defining Tasks and in the tables at the end of this page.

docs.title: Class Options: Shared by Every Task
docs.text:
class_option declares an option once for every task in the class. A --dry-run or --env that applies to the whole project belongs here:

class Tasks
  class_option :dry_run, aliases: "-n", type: :boolean, default: false, desc: "Print commands without running them"
  class_option :env,     type: :string, default: "development", enum: %w[development staging production], desc: "Target environment"

  desc "Deploy the application"
  def deploy
    if options.dry_run?
      puts "Would deploy to #{options.env}"
    else
      sh "cap #{options.env} deploy"
    end
  end

  desc "Run database migrations"
  def migrate = sh "rails db:migrate RAILS_ENV=#{options[:env]}"
end

asgard deploy --env staging --dry-run
asgard migrate --env production
asgard help migrate          # lists --dry-run and --env under Options

Options come after the task name, class options included: asgard deploy --env staging works, asgard --env staging deploy does not (asgard sees no task name and complains that help got unexpected arguments). The two exceptions are --version and --doctor, which are asgard's own flags and come first.

docs.title: Class Options and Subcommands
docs.text:
A subcommand class written as class DBCommands < Tasks inherits every class option declared on Tasks, including asgard's own. Declare new ones in the subcommand class for options only its tasks need.

Warning

Do not declare class_option :debug or class_option :verbose (or :version, :doctor) in a subcommand class. They are already inherited, and a second declaration raises an error about a duplicate option. See Subcommands.

docs.title: Boolean Class Options and no_negate
docs.text:
For every boolean class option, the help lists three spellings: [--color], [--no-color] and [--skip-color]. When negating the option makes no sense, call no_negate after the declaration to show only the plain flag:

class Tasks
  class_option :color, type: :boolean, default: true, desc: "Colorize output"
  no_negate :color
end

Help before:

[--color], [--no-color], [--skip-color]  # Colorize output

Help after:

[--color]                                # Colorize output

no_negate takes several names at once, no_negate :color, :emoji, and only changes the help text: --no-color still works if someone types it.

docs.title: Built-in Flags
docs.text:
Four flags are available on every task. They appear under Options: in asgard help.

Flag What it does When it acts --version Prints asgard's version and exits Before any task file loads; works with no project --doctor Prints a diagnosis of the project's task files and exits Before the normal startup, so it works even when a .loki is broken --debug Sets $DEBUG to true, so debug? is true Before the task body runs --verbose Sets $VERBOSE to true, so verbose? is true Before the task body runs 
asgard --version
asgard --doctor
asgard build --debug
asgard build --verbose
asgard build --debug --verbose

Where each flag goes

--version and --doctor come first, before any task name. After a task name they are the task's own arguments: asgard mytask --version runs mytask and passes --version to it, which lets a task of yours define its own --version option. --debug and --verbose are ordinary class options and go after the task name, like every other option.

docs.title: --version
docs.text:
asgard --version

0.6.0

docs.title: --doctor
docs.text:
asgard --doctor

Prints which .loki was used, what each import loaded, every task grouped by the file that defines it with a file:line an editor can jump to, any task defined twice (the earlier one is silently dead), hidden tasks, and any dependency problem. It runs even when the normal startup would abort on a broken file. The report is explained line by line on Help & Diagnostics.

docs.title: --debug and --verbose
docs.text:
Both set a Ruby global before the task runs, and the predicates debug? and verbose? read it back. They are also ordinary class options, so options.debug? and options.verbose? work and are always true or false:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build
    puts "options: #{options.inspect}" if debug?
    sh "rake build#{' --trace' if verbose?}"
  end
end

asgard build --verbose

rake build --trace
...

The flags also trace an import that runs inside a task body. With --verbose, such an import prints each file it loads on standard error; add --debug to also see a file it skipped because it was already loaded, and an import_up that found nothing:

asgard build --verbose --debug

import: /home/you/myproject/extra.loki
import: skip /home/you/myproject/extra.loki (already loaded)
import_up: team_tasks.loki not found

The imports at the top of .loki run before the task name is read, so the flags cannot trace them. To see every file as it loads, run with Ruby's warning switch, RUBYOPT=-w asgard build, or use asgard --doctor; see Task Files.

debug? and verbose? work everywhere in a .loki: in task bodies, in helpers, and in the class body. Note that --debug, --verbose and a task's own options are parsed only once the task is chosen, which is why a depends_on block cannot see them (next section).

docs.title: Where options Is Available
docs.text:
options is the parsed command line of the task being run. It is available:

  • inside the task body;
  • inside a helper method called from the task body (private methods, no_commands methods, helper methods);
  • inside a dependency's body, where it holds the same values: a dependency sees the options given to the task you typed, since the whole run shares one command line.

It is not available:

  • in the class body, where desc, option and @@ variables are declared, because no command line has been parsed yet;
  • inside a depends_on { ... } block, which runs while the task files are being validated, before the command line is parsed (see Dependencies).

For a value a task needs at class-load time, read an environment variable with env instead; see Environment Variables.

docs.title: DSL Reference
docs.text:
Every word you can write in a .loki file, on one page. Each entry gives the signature, what it does in one line, a one-line example, and a link to the guide page that explains it in full. Use this page to look something up; use the guide pages to learn it.

A .loki file is plain Ruby that reopens class Tasks. Asgard is built on Thor, so Thor's own DSL words (desc, method_option, class_option, long_desc, map, subcommand, default_task, argument, no_commands) work inside it, alongside asgard's own.

docs.title: Names You Cannot Use
docs.text:
• Names Thor uses internally. Defining a task or helper called shell, options, invoke, run, args, behavior, root, destination_root, action, in_root, inside or parent_options (among others on Thor's reserved list) stops asgard as the .loki loads, with the file and line. Pick another name. This is why the watcher's foreground command is spelled asgard watcher run while your own task cannot be named run.
  • Names beginning with _. The underscore prefix is reserved for asgard's own built-ins. asgard _anything is refused as an unknown command, and a .loki must not define _-prefixed methods.
  • schedule, watcher, jobs. You may define tasks with these names, but asgard schedule, asgard watcher and asgard jobs still run the built-ins.
  • A name defined twice. The later def silently replaces the earlier one; asgard --doctor reports it. See Task Files.

docs.title: Return Values and Exit Status
docs.text:
What happens Asgard exits with The task you typed finishes normally 0 The task you typed returns the symbol :fail 1 (:warn, :skip and every other value exit 0) A sh or shebang script exits non-zero that status, at once A script is ended by a signal 128 plus the signal number The shell or interpreter cannot be found 127 raise Asgard::Error, "msg" or abort "msg" 1, after printing the message A usage error (missing argument, unknown task or option) 1 A .loki fails to load, or a dependency graph is invalid 1, after one line of explanation Ctrl-C 130

A dependency's return value never stops the task that depends on it; only an exit, an abort or a raise does. Full detail in Help & Diagnostics and Dependencies.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Any task can run on a timer. You say when in the project's .loki with a schedule line, and asgard schedule install hands the entry to the scheduler your operating system already has: launchd on macOS, systemd user timers on Linux. From then on the task runs whether or not a terminal is open, and a run that was missed while the machine slept happens as soon as it wakes.

Scheduling is built in. There is nothing to install or require beyond asgard itself.

docs.title: The Shortest Example
docs.text:
# .loki
class Tasks
  desc "Summarize the day's work"
  def daily_summary = sh "bin/summary"

  schedule :daily_summary, at: "17:30", on: :weekdays
end

asgard schedule install

installed daily_summary: asgard daily_summary (17:30 weekdays)

That is a working schedule. Every weekday at 17:30 the scheduler runs asgard daily_summary in the directory that holds .loki, and its output goes to a log you can read with asgard schedule log daily_summary.

A schedule declaration in .loki is installed into launchd or systemd, which runs the task in the project root and appends its output to a log file.

.loki schedule :report, options: "--period week", at: "16:00", on: :friday

asgard schedule install writes the job files, loads them

launchd / systemd fires every Friday at 16:00 (or on wake, if the machine slept)

asgard report --period week in the project root, with the PATH captured at install and env:

log file asgard schedule log report-period-week

stdout + stderr

A declaration in .loki is installed into the platform scheduler, which runs the task in the project root and appends its output to a log.

docs.title: Declaring Schedules
docs.text:
schedule goes at class level inside Tasks, next to the tasks it names. A declaration needs exactly one of at: (a time of day) or every: (an interval).

class Tasks
  schedule :daily_summary, at: "17:30", on: :weekdays
  schedule :weekly_report, at: "16:00", on: :friday
  schedule :sync,          every: 3600                 # seconds
  schedule :backup,        at: %w[02:00 14:00]         # on: defaults to :daily
  schedule :heartbeat,     at: "09:00", on: %i[monday thursday]

  # The task's own command-line options go in options:
  schedule :report, options: "--format md -v",      at: "08:00", on: :weekdays
  schedule :report, options: "--period week",       at: "16:00", on: :friday
  schedule :notify, options: "--msg 'backup done'", every: 86_400, as: "notify_daily"
end
Keyword Meaning at: A time of day as "HH:MM" (24-hour clock), or an Array of them on: Which days at: applies to: :daily (the default), :weekdays, :weekends, one day such as :friday, or an Array of days every: An interval in seconds, or any object that answers in_seconds (an ActiveSupport Duration) options: The task's own arguments and flags, as one String split the way a shell would (quotes respected) or as an Array of words env: { "KEY" => "value" }: environment variables added to the job as: The entry's name (see Entry Names)

docs.title: Times and Days
docs.text:
at: takes one time or several. on: chooses the days; leave it out for every day.

schedule :backup, at: "02:00"                          # every day at 02:00
schedule :backup, at: %w[02:00 14:00]                  # twice a day
schedule :standup, at: "09:25", on: :weekdays
schedule :cleanup, at: "23:00", on: :weekends
schedule :review,  at: "16:00", on: %i[tuesday thursday]

A time that is not HH:MM, an hour above 23, a minute above 59, an unknown day name, or an empty Array are all rejected when the .loki loads, with a message that names the problem:

asgard: /proj/.loki:9: at: expects "HH:MM" (got "5pm") (ArgumentError)
asgard: /proj/.loki:10: on: unknown day :funday (ArgumentError)

docs.title: Intervals
docs.text:
every: runs the task repeatedly, one interval after the scheduler starts it and one interval after each run. It takes a number of seconds:

schedule :sync, every: 900        # every 15 minutes
schedule :poll, every: 60 * 60    # Ruby arithmetic is fine

Asgard does not depend on ActiveSupport, but it accepts anything that answers in_seconds, so 15.minutes works once you require it yourself at the top of the .loki:

require "active_support/core_ext/integer/time"

class Tasks
  schedule :sync, every: 15.minutes
end

An interval that is zero, negative or not a number is rejected: schedule :sync every: must be a positive number of seconds or a Duration (3.minutes).

docs.title: Options for the Task
docs.text:
The scheduler runs asgard <task> with nothing else unless you say otherwise. options: carries the task's own arguments and flags. A String is split the way a shell splits a command line, so quotes group words:

schedule :report, options: "--format md --title 'Week End'", at: "16:00", on: :friday
schedule :report, options: %w[--format md --since 2026-01-01], at: "08:00"

Both forms run the task with each word passed as its own argument, so nothing is re-split or re-quoted on the way to the task. Newlines and other control characters are not allowed in options: or in env: values, because the job files are line-based.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
env: adds literal variables to the job. Keys must be valid variable names (letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit).

schedule :deploy_docs, at: "03:00", env: { "SITE_ENV" => "production", "VERBOSE" => "1" }

Secrets do not belong here, because env: values are written into the job file. Put them in a .envrc instead and let direnv load them at run time. See Environment Variables for what a scheduled task sees.

docs.title: Entry Names
docs.text:
Every declaration becomes an entry with a name, and every asgard schedule subcommand that acts on one entry takes that name as NAME.

Declaration Entry name schedule :daily_summary, at: "17:30" daily_summary schedule :report, options: "--format md -v", at: "08:00" report-format-md-v schedule :report, options: "--period week", at: "16:00" report-period-week schedule :notify, options: "--msg 'backup done'", every: 86_400, as: "notify_daily" notify_daily

The name defaults to the task name. When the entry has options:, the default is a slug of the task plus its options, so one task can be scheduled several times with different flags and each run has its own entry, state and log. as: replaces the default with a name you choose; it may contain letters, digits, _, . and -.

Two different declarations that end up with the same name are an error when the .loki loads:

asgard: /proj/.loki:12: schedule: "report" is already declared; give one a distinct as: name (ArgumentError)

(Loading the same declaration twice, as happens when a file is imported from two places, is fine.)

docs.title: Task Names with Dashes and Subcommands
docs.text:
A task is always one word. A dash in it is taken as the underscore of the method name, so schedule :daily-summary schedules the daily_summary task. A subcommand's task cannot be named with a colon; schedule the subcommand itself and put the rest in options::

schedule :db, options: "migrate --dry-run", at: "02:00"   # runs: asgard db migrate --dry-run

Writing schedule :"db:migrate" is rejected with exactly that advice.

docs.title: Managing Schedules
docs.text:
schedule is also a command with subcommands. They work the same way on macOS and Linux.

asgard schedule preview        # print the job files install would write
asgard schedule install        # install declared entries; remove this project's undeclared ones
asgard schedule list           # this project's entries, their state and last exit
asgard schedule list --all     # every project's entries
asgard schedule log NAME       # print the entry's log
asgard schedule log NAME -f    # keep following it
asgard schedule trigger NAME   # run an installed entry now
asgard schedule stop NAME      # stop one entry; it stays stopped until started
asgard schedule start NAME     # start a stopped entry, or install just this one
asgard schedule remove [NAME]  # remove one entry, or all of this project's
asgard schedule prune          # remove every project's entries whose directory is gone

The rest of this section walks through each one with the .loki from the declaration example.

docs.title: install
docs.text:
install writes the job files for every declared entry, loads them, and removes any entry of this project that is installed but no longer declared. It prints one line per entry:

asgard schedule install

installed daily_summary: asgard daily_summary (17:30 weekdays)
installed weekly_report: asgard weekly_report (16:00 friday)
installed sync: asgard sync (every 3600s)
installed backup: asgard backup (02:00, 14:00 daily)
installed report-format-md-v: asgard report --format md -v (08:00 weekdays)
installed report-period-week: asgard report --period week (16:00 friday)
installed notify_daily: asgard notify --msg 'backup done' (every 86400s)

An entry you stopped earlier is reinstalled but left stopped, and the line says so: installed sync: ... [stopped;asgard schedule start syncto resume]. An entry that was removed from .loki prints removed NAME.

install refuses to run when a declaration names a task the project does not define (schedule: no such task(s): nightly), when there are no declarations at all, or when asgard itself is not on your PATH. On Linux it ends with a note about lingering when your user timers would stop at logout (see Platforms).

Run install again whenever you change a declaration, or whenever your PATH changes (a new Ruby, a new Homebrew prefix). The job keeps the PATH that was current at install time, nothing else.

│ report-format-md-v    │ asgard report --format md -v       │ 08:00 weekdays   │ running    │ 0         │
│ report-period-week    │ asgard report --period week        │ 16:00 friday     │ active     │ 1         │
│ sync                  │ asgard sync                        │ every 3600s      │ not loaded │ -         │
│ weekly_report         │ asgard weekly_report               │ 16:00 friday     │ active     │ 0         │
└───────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────┴───────────┘

Logs: /Users/you/Library/Logs/asgard  (asgard schedule log NAME)
STATE Meaning active Installed and waiting for its next time running The task is running right now stopped Stopped with asgard schedule stop; it will not fire until started not loaded The job files exist but the scheduler does not have the entry loaded (a reboot that did not reload it, a hand edit); asgard schedule install fixes it

LAST EXIT is the exit status of the last run (0 is success), never run for an active entry that has not fired yet, or - for an entry that is stopped or not loaded. On macOS a run ended by a signal shows as signal 15 (Terminated). A non-zero status is shown in red on a terminal; set NO_COLOR to turn colour off. Long COMMAND and SCHEDULE cells wrap to the terminal width, and a run of hourly times collapses to 10:00-17:00 hourly weekdays.

An entry that is installed but no longer in .loki shows no longer declared in the SCHEDULE column until the next install removes it.

With nothing installed:

No scheduled tasks installed for api-9f3a1c2b (launchd).
Use `asgard schedule list --all` to see all currently scheduled tasks.

docs.title: log
docs.text:
Each entry appends the stdout and stderr of every run to its own log file. log NAME prints it; -f keeps printing as new output arrives, like tail -f:

asgard schedule log daily_summary
asgard schedule log daily_summary -f

An entry that has never run has no log yet: daily_summary has no log yet (/Users/you/Library/Logs/asgard/...log); it is created on the first run.

docs.title: trigger
docs.text:
trigger NAME runs an installed entry right now, under the scheduler and with the scheduler's environment, which makes it the honest way to test a schedule: a task that works at your prompt but fails under trigger has a PATH or environment problem, not a code problem.

asgard schedule trigger daily_summary

triggered daily_summary; output goes to /Users/you/Library/Logs/asgard/com.madbomber.asgard.api-9f3a1c2b.daily_summary.log

A stopped entry is refused: daily_summary is stopped;asgard schedule start daily_summaryfirst.

docs.title: stop and start
docs.text:
stop NAME stops one entry. The stop is remembered: the entry stays stopped across reboots and across later install runs, until you start it.

asgard schedule stop sync
# stopped sync
asgard schedule start sync
# started sync

start NAME does two things. For an entry that is declared in this project's .loki it refreshes the job files from the current declaration and installs just that one entry, whether or not it was installed before; so start is also the way to install a single new entry without touching the others. For an entry that is installed but no longer declared, or that belongs to another project, it starts the installed job as it is and says so on stderr: schedule: sync is no longer declared; starting its installed job as-is.

docs.title: remove
docs.text:
remove NAME unloads and deletes one entry's job files and forgets any stop. remove with no name does that for every entry of this project:

asgard schedule remove sync
# removed sync
asgard schedule remove
# removed backup
# removed daily_summary
# ...

The log files are left in place.

docs.title: prune
docs.text:
A project that was moved or deleted leaves its entries behind, and they keep firing in a directory that is not there. prune removes every such entry, from every project on the machine. --dry-run (-n) only lists them:

asgard schedule prune --dry-run
# would remove api-9f3a1c2b/daily_summary
asgard schedule prune
# removed api-9f3a1c2b/daily_summary

With nothing to do it prints Nothing to prune: every installed entry's project directory exists.

docs.title: Every Project at Once
docs.text:
list --all (-a) shows every project's entries, grouped under a title that names the project and its directory. Other projects' .loki files are not loaded; their columns are read back from the installed job files.

asgard schedule list --all

Project: api-9f3a1c2b (/Users/you/work/api)
┌───────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────┬────────┬───────────┐
│ NAME          │ COMMAND              │ SCHEDULE       │ STATE  │ LAST EXIT │
├───────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ daily_summary │ asgard daily_summary │ 17:30 weekdays │ active │ 0         │
└───────────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────┴────────┴───────────┘

Project: blog-13ab77e0 (/Users/you/old/blog) [root missing]
┌─────────┬────────────────┬─────────────┬────────┬───────────┐
│ NAME    │ COMMAND        │ SCHEDULE    │ STATE  │ LAST EXIT │
├─────────┼────────────────┼─────────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ publish │ asgard publish │ 06:00 daily │ active │ 127       │
└─────────┴────────────────┴─────────────┴────────┴───────────┘

Logs: /Users/you/Library/Logs/asgard  (asgard schedule log NAME)

[root missing] marks a project whose directory no longer exists; prune removes its entries. Run from a directory with no .loki above it, list shows every project without needing --all.

docs.title: Reaching Another Project's Entry
docs.text:
stop, start, trigger, log and remove accept an entry of any project, so they work from any directory. Name it as project/name, where project is the slug shown by list --all, or just the directory name when that is enough to pick one project out:

asgard schedule stop blog/publish            # the directory name is enough
asgard schedule stop blog-13ab77e0/publish   # the full slug always works
asgard schedule log api/daily_summary -f

A bare name is looked up in this project first, then in every other project. When two other projects share a name, asgard asks you to be specific: publish is in several projects (blog-13ab77e0, blog-9c0f22d1); name one as project/publish.

docs.title: How Jobs Run
docs.text:
Each entry runs asgard <task> [options] from the directory that holds .loki, so it does not matter which subdirectory you ran install from. The job's environment is small and fixed:

  • PATH as it was when you ran install. A scheduler does not read your shell's startup files, so this is the only PATH the job has. Re-run install after changing it.
  • The declaration's env: variables.
  • If the project has a .envrc, the job is wrapped in direnv exec, so the variables in .envrc (API keys, credentials) are loaded at run time and never copied into the job files. If direnv is not on your PATH, install warns: schedule: .envrc found but direnv is not on PATH; its variables will not be loaded.
  • Whatever the task's own .loki loads with dotenv, since that runs inside the task's process as usual.

The job's stdout and stderr are appended to its log file.

A calendar entry (at:) that was due while the machine was asleep or off runs as soon as the machine is back; on macOS launchd does this on wake, and on Linux the timer is Persistent. An interval entry (every:) simply resumes its cadence.

docs.title: The Project Slug
docs.text:
Entries belong to a project, and the project is named by a slug: the name of the directory holding .loki plus a short hash of that directory's full path, such as api-9f3a1c2b. Two projects in directories with the same name therefore never share entries, and install in one can never remove the other's. The slug is stable as long as the project stays where it is; a moved project gets a new slug, and its old entries show up under [root missing] until you prune them and install again from the new location.

The slug appears in the job file names, the log file names and the list --all titles.

docs.title: Shells Under the Scheduler
docs.text:
The PATH a job sees is rarely the one your terminal has. On a Mac with Homebrew, bash at the terminal is 5.x from /opt/homebrew/bin, while under launchd it may be the 3.2 build in /bin. If a task's script needs a particular interpreter, pin it in the .loki so the same one runs everywhere:

class Tasks
  shell :bash, "/opt/homebrew/bin/bash"
end

See Shell Commands.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
macOS (launchd) Linux (systemd) Job files ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.madbomber.asgard.<slug>.<name>.plist ~/.config/systemd/user/asgard.<slug>.<name>.service and .timer (honours XDG_CONFIG_HOME) Logs ~/Library/Logs/asgard/com.madbomber.asgard.<slug>.<name>.log ~/.local/state/asgard/asgard.<slug>.<name>.log (honours XDG_STATE_HOME) stop launchctl disable plus unload; remembered by launchd systemctl --user disable --now on the timer Missed runs Run on wake Persistent=true on calendar timers Runs while logged out? No; user agents run only while you are logged in Only after loginctl enable-linger; install prints a reminder when lingering is off Requirements systemd 240 or later

Any other platform is unsupported: every asgard schedule subcommand there exits with asgard: <platform> is not supported (needs macOS launchd or Linux systemd).

Job files are written readable by you alone, since they can hold env: values. On macOS a plist is checked with plutil before it replaces the installed one, and an unchanged plist whose job is already loaded is left alone by install, so a reinstall never interrupts a run in progress.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The job never runs. Check asgard schedule list. stopped means a stop is in effect: start it. not loaded means the scheduler lost the entry: install again. On macOS, user agents run only while you are logged in; on Linux, run loginctl enable-linger or the timers stop when you log out. trigger NAME runs the entry right now under the scheduler, which tells you whether the job itself works.

schedule: asgard is not on PATH. install needs to write the absolute path of asgard into the job. Make sure the directory holding the asgard executable (your Ruby's gem bin directory) is on PATH in the shell you run install from.

schedule: .envrc found but direnv is not on PATH; its variables will not be loaded. The project has a .envrc, but the job cannot load it without direnv. Install direnv and run install again, or move the variables the task needs into env:.

The job fails with command not found after a Ruby or Homebrew upgrade. The job still has the PATH from the day you installed it. Run asgard schedule install again to capture the current one.

The task works at the prompt but fails under the scheduler. The job's environment is only PATH, env: and .envrc; nothing from your shell's startup files reaches it. Run asgard schedule trigger NAME and read asgard schedule log NAME to see the actual error. See Environment Variables.

schedule: no such task(s): x. A declaration names a task that no loaded .loki defines. Check the spelling, and check that the file defining it is imported (see Task Files).

docs.title: Name Collisions
docs.text: The built-in command is registered under a reserved name and mapped to schedule. If your .loki defines its own task called schedule, asgard schedule still runs the built-in; name your task something else.

docs.title: Shell Commands
docs.text:
Some asgard tasks need to run processes that are not executed in Ruby: a build, a test suite, a deploy script, a Python one-off. Asgard gives every task one method for that, under two names: sh and shebang are the same method, and everything on this page about one is true of the other. sh :python3, script runs the script under the interpreter registered as :python3; sh script, with no shell named, runs it under the default shell. Many task authors write sh without a shell designation as the short-cut for an ordinary shell command and reserve the longer shebang for scripts in another language, which is how this page is laid out, but that is a habit, not a rule.

Whichever spelling you use, the script is written to a temporary file, run, and asgard stops if it fails, so a pipeline of tasks never continues past a broken step.

Start with the nameless form. Everything else on this page is a refinement of it.

docs.title: sh: Run a Script in the Default Shell
docs.text:
sh takes a script and runs it. One line or many, it works the same way:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build = sh "rake build"

  desc "Check for a Gemfile"
  def check = sh '[[ -f Gemfile ]] && echo "found"'

  desc "Bootstrap the development environment"
  def setup
    sh <<~SHELL
      brew install redis postgresql
      brew services start redis
      bundle install
      rails db:setup
    SHELL
  end
end

asgard build

rake build
... rake's output ...

The script is printed before it runs, so the terminal shows what asgard did. All lines of a heredoc run in one shell session, so a variable set on one line is visible on the next:

desc "Tag the build"
def tag
  sh <<~SHELL
    version=$(cat VERSION)
    git tag "v$version"
    echo "tagged v$version"
  SHELL
end

The shell is bash until a .loki says otherwise (see default_shell). Bash syntax such as [[ ... ]], arrays and $PIPESTATUS works in a one-liner as well as in a heredoc.

Note

Before 0.6.0 a one-line sh went through /bin/sh and a heredoc through bash, so bash syntax passed or failed depending on line count. Both now take the same path. See Upgrading to 0.6.0.

docs.title: Silent Mode
docs.text:
Pass silent: true to skip the echo. The script still runs and still stops asgard on failure:

desc "Compile (quiet)"
def build = sh "rake build", silent: true

docs.title: Exit on Failure
docs.text:
When the script exits non-zero, asgard exits with that same status. Nothing after the failing sh runs, no Ruby exception is raised, and there is nothing to rescue:

class Tasks
  depends_on :test
  desc "Test then release"
  def release
    sh "bundle exec rake release"
    puts "Released!"        # never reached if rake release fails
  end
end

asgard release; echo "exit $?"
# ... rake release fails with status 1 ...
# exit 1

A command that ends on a signal exits with 128 plus the signal number, the way a shell reports it. This is deliberate: a task runner that continued past a failed step would hide the failure. When a command is allowed to fail, say so in the script or in Ruby:

desc "Remove build output, if any"
def clean
  sh "rm -r dist || true"                  # the shell swallows the failure
end

desc "Report whether the server is up"
def ping
  if system("curl -fsS localhost:3000/health > /dev/null")   # plain Ruby: returns true or false
    puts "up"
  else
    puts "down"
  end
end

desc "Count TODO comments"
def todos
  count = `grep -r TODO lib | wc -l`.strip   # backticks capture output, never exit asgard
  puts "#{count} TODOs"
end

sh returns true when the script succeeds, which is useful at the end of an endless-method task: def build = sh "rake build".

docs.title: shebang: Any Interpreter
docs.text:
shebang :name, script writes the script to a tempfile with the extension registered for name and runs the registered executable on it. Python, Node, Ruby, Perl or anything else can live directly in a task:

class Tasks
  desc "Run Python data analysis"
  def analyze
    shebang :python3, <<~PYTHON
      import json
      data = json.load(open("results.json"))
      print(f"Total: {sum(data.values())}")
    PYTHON
  end

  desc "Build frontend assets with esbuild"
  def bundle_assets
    shebang :node, <<~JS
      import * as esbuild from "esbuild"
      esbuild.buildSync({ entryPoints: ["src/app.js"], bundle: true, outfile: "dist/app.js" })
    JS
  end

  desc "Run a bash provisioning script"
  def provision
    shebang :bash, <<~BASH
      set -euo pipefail
      apt-get update
      apt-get install -y curl wget git
    BASH
  end
end

shebang is the same method as sh, so it takes the same silent: and background: keywords, echoes the script the same way, and exits asgard on failure the same way. sh :python3, script and shebang :python3, script are one call; so are shebang "rake build" and sh "rake build".

docs.title: Interpreters You Did Not Register
docs.text:
A name that is not in the registry runs as itself, found on PATH, with a .tmp file extension. Any interpreter works without declaring it:

desc "Say hello from Lua"
def lua_hello = shebang :lua, 'print("Hello from Lua!")'

If the executable is not found, asgard names the shell and the command it tried, then exits 127:

asgard: shell :lua not found: lua /var/folders/.../T/asgard_20261024-80545-1x2y3z.tmp

Register the interpreter with shell when it needs a specific extension or options, or when you want the mistake caught while the .loki loads rather than the first time the task runs.

docs.title: The shells Registry
docs.text:
Every shell name maps to an executable, the arguments placed before the script file, and the tempfile extension. The registry starts with these entries:

Name Executable Arguments Extension :bash bash none .sh :sh sh none .sh :python3 python3 none .py :python python none .py :node node none .js :ruby ruby none .rb :perl perl none .pl

You can read an entry back in a .loki:

Tasks.shells[:bash]   # => { path: "bash", args: [], ext: ".sh" }

A bare executable such as bash is looked up on PATH each time a script runs, exactly as a #!/usr/bin/env bash line would do. The extension matters only to interpreters that read it: Node decides between CommonJS and ES modules by extension, and PowerShell refuses a script that is not .ps1. Zsh and fish scripts get .sh and .fish even without a registry entry, and csh and tcsh get .csh.

There is one registry for the whole project. A shell declared in .loki applies inside subcommand classes too.

docs.title: shell: Add or Replace an Entry
docs.text:
shell at class level registers a shell and returns its name. The simplest forms name the shell and give its path:

class Tasks
  shell :bash,   "/opt/homebrew/bin/bash"           # pin bash 5 for sh and shebang :bash
  shell :strict, "bash -eu -o pipefail"             # options before the script
  shell :uv,     "uv run --script", ext: ".py"      # a wrapper command, not just a binary
  shell :fish                                       # fish from PATH, defaults

  desc "Deploy under strict bash"
  def deploy = shebang :strict, <<~BASH
    cd build
    rsync -a . server:/srv/app/
  BASH
end

Tasks.shells[:strict]  # => { path: "bash", args: ["-eu", "-o", "pipefail"], ext: ".sh" }

The path string is split the way a shell splits a command line, quotes respected: the first word is the executable and the rest become arguments. args: adds more arguments, as a String (also split) or an Array; they follow the words from the path. ext: sets the tempfile extension; when omitted it comes from the executable's basename (.sh for bash, .py for python3, and so on), falling back to .tmp.

These are all the same entry:

shell :strict, "bash -eu -o pipefail"
shell :strict, "bash", args: "-eu -o pipefail"
shell :strict, "bash", args: %w[-eu -o pipefail]

Leaving the name out. A bare path registers under the executable's basename, with any options parsed into the arguments:

shell "/usr/local/bin/bash -c -w"      # :bash => { path: "/usr/local/bin/bash", args: ["-c", "-w"], ext: ".sh" }
shell Pathname.new("/opt/homebrew/bin/fish")   # :fish

Paths with spaces. A Pathname is one executable, taken whole and never split, so a directory with a space in it needs no quoting:

shell :tool, "'/Applications/Some App/bin/tool' -q"                           # quoted String
shell :tool, Pathname.new("/Applications/Some App/bin/tool"), args: "-q"      # same entry, no quoting

The executable is checked as the .loki loads. A path with a directory part must be an existing executable file, exactly as written (nothing expands ~ or searches PATH for it later). A bare name must be found on PATH. A failing check stops the load with a message naming the shell:

asgard: /proj/.loki:3: shell :bash: /opt/homebrew/bin/bash is not an executable file (ArgumentError)
asgard: /proj/.loki:4: shell :uv: uv is not an executable on PATH (ArgumentError)

This is why a typo in a shell line shows at startup, while a missing seeded interpreter (shebang :perl on a machine without perl) shows only when the task runs: the seeded entries are not checked until they are used.

docs.title: default_shell: The Shell Used When None Is Named
docs.text:
default_shell picks the registry entry that sh and shebang run when no shell is named. It starts as :bash. With no argument it returns the current name.

A bare Symbol only selects. It checks that the shell exists but never changes the registry, so a path pinned earlier with shell stays pinned:

class Tasks
  shell :strict, "bash -eu -o pipefail"
  default_shell :strict

  desc "Every call that names no shell now runs under strict bash"
  def build
    sh "rake build"              # no shell named: runs under :strict
    shebang "rake package"       # same shell, same path
    shebang :python3, "print('an explicit name still wins')"
  end
end

Any other form registers first, exactly as shell would, then selects what it registered:

class Tasks
  default_shell "/usr/local/bin/bash -c -w"                # register :bash with those options, select it
  default_shell :strict, "bash", args: "-eu -o pipefail"   # register :strict, select it
  default_shell :zsh, args: "-f"                           # path defaults to the name, "zsh"
  default_shell :bash5, Pathname.new("/opt/homebrew/bin/bash")
end

Like the registry, the default is one value for the whole project, subcommands included. A .loki that imports several files should set it once, in the root .loki, before the imports.

docs.title: Pinning a Path
docs.text:
Your terminal's PATH and the PATH a scheduled or watched task sees are not the same. On a Mac with Homebrew, bash at the terminal is 5.x from /opt/homebrew/bin, while a job started by launchd finds the 3.2 build in /bin. A script that uses associative arrays or ${var,,} works in one and fails in the other. Pin the one you mean:

shell :bash, "/opt/homebrew/bin/bash"

A .loki is Ruby, so a path that differs between machines is an ordinary expression:

shell :bash, %w[/opt/homebrew/bin/bash /usr/local/bin/bash /bin/bash].find { File.executable?(it) }

docs.title: Long-Running Commands
docs.text:
A dev server, a REPL or a watch loop needs nothing special. Asgard waits for the shell, the shell waits for the command, and Ctrl-C reaches all three at once because they share the terminal's process group:

class Tasks
  desc "Serve the documentation"
  depends_on :doc_builder
  def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve"

  desc "Start a REPL"
  def console = sh "bundle exec pry"
end

asgard doc_server
# ... Ctrl-C ...
# asgard exits 130

Asgard exits with the shell's status, so a command that ends on a signal exits 128 plus the signal number.

Note

Earlier versions accepted exec: true to replace the asgard process with the command. It was removed in 0.6.0 and now raises ArgumentError (unknown keyword: :exec); delete the keyword. See Upgrading to 0.6.0.

docs.title: $0 Is a Tempfile
docs.text: Because the script runs from a file, $0 inside it is the path of that tempfile, such as /var/folders/.../T/asgard_20261024-80545-bmbloc.sh, and the file is deleted when the script ends. A usage message that printed $0 should print a name you choose instead.

docs.title: Three Ways a Script Runs
docs.text:
A script runs in one of three modes. The first two are asgard's; the third belongs to the shell.

Mode How you ask for it The task When asgard exits asgard jobs Foreground sh "rake build" Waits for the script before its next statement; a failure exits asgard The script has already finished Nothing to manage Managed background sh "mkdocs serve", background: true Continues at once with a job object in hand The job keeps running Lists, stops, restarts and cleans it Detached sh "mkdocs serve &" Continues at once with true; the shell has already exited The process keeps running Knows nothing about it

background: true names the job after the calling task plus a counter (doc_server-1); a Symbol or String names it outright (background: :api). The job starts in its own session with its output in a log file, its pid and task are recorded, and asgard jobs list|stop|log|restart|clean manage it from then on, in this asgard run or any later one:

class Tasks
  desc "Serve the documentation"
  depends_on :doc_builder
  def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve", background: true

  desc "Bring up the development stack"
  def servers
    sh "docker compose up postgres", background: true    # servers-1
    sh "bin/rails server",            background: :api   # api
  end
end

asgard doc_server

mkdocs serve
started doc_server-1 (pid 48213), log: ~/.local/state/asgard/jobs/asgard-5d41402a/doc_server-1.log

A trailing & in a script is not a managed job. The shell detaches the process and exits, asgard reports success and keeps no record, and the process runs on with its output still in your terminal. You stop it yourself with ps and kill. Use background: for anything you expect to come back to. The whole story, including naming rules, the commands and the files on disk, is on the Background Jobs page.

docs.title: Combining sh and shebang
docs.text:
Mix both freely in one task. Each call runs to completion before the next starts:

class Tasks
  desc "Run a mixed shell and Python pipeline"
  def pipeline
    sh "bundle exec rake build"

    shebang :python3, <<~PYTHON
      import subprocess
      result = subprocess.run(["./bin/validate"], capture_output=True, text=True)
      print(result.stdout)
    PYTHON

    sh "rake deploy"
  end
end

Because every call stops asgard on failure, the Python step never runs after a failed build and the deploy never runs after failed validation. To share values between steps, write them to a file or an environment variable in the script, or compute them in Ruby and interpolate them into the next script (see Variables).

docs.title: sh Versus Ruby's Own Methods
docs.text:
A .loki is Ruby, so everything Ruby offers for running a program works in a task: system, backticks, %x(), exec, spawn, Open3.capture3. Nothing stops you using them, and the examples above do. What sh and shebang add is the behaviour a task runner needs around the command:

sh / shebang system Backticks Shows the command before running it Yes, unless silent: true No No On failure Exits asgard with the command's status; nothing after it runs Returns false and the task carries on Returns the output and the task carries on Missing interpreter Prints which shell and exits 127 Returns nil Raises Errno::ENOENT Ended by a signal Exits 128 plus the signal number Returns false Returns partial output Which shell runs it The one registered in shells, the same under the watcher and a schedule /bin/sh, or none for a single word /bin/sh One line or a heredoc The same path either way A heredoc runs as one /bin/sh script Same Other interpreters shebang :python3, script Build the argv yourself Same As a managed background job background: true No No Returns true, or a job object true, false or nil The command's stdout

The first two rows are the reason to prefer sh by default. A task that calls system("rake test") and does not check the return value continues to the release step whether the tests passed or not, and asgard exits 0. The same line as sh "rake test" stops at the failure and exits with rake's status, and the log shows which command it was. Under the watcher and a schedule, where nobody is watching the terminal, both matter more.

The shell row is the other one worth knowing. system and backticks go through /bin/sh, which is dash on Debian and Ubuntu and bash 3.2 in POSIX mode on macOS, so bash syntax that works at your prompt may not work there. sh runs the :bash entry of the shells registry, and shell :bash, "/opt/homebrew/bin/bash" pins it to one executable for every run on the machine.

Ruby's methods are still the right tool when you want the output as a value, or when a failure is information rather than an error:

desc "Tag the release"
def tag
  version = `git describe --tags --abbrev=0`.strip     # capture: backticks
  sh "git tag #{version.succ} && git push --tags"      # act: sh
end

desc "Report whether the server is up"
def ping
  puts system("curl -fsS localhost:3000/health > /dev/null") ? "up" : "down"   # false is an answer, not a failure
end

sh never captures output: the script's stdout and stderr go straight to yours, or to the watcher, schedule or job log. To use a command's output in Ruby, use backticks or Open3; to run a step that must succeed, use sh.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Call What it runs Notes sh "script" The default shell (:bash until changed) One line or heredoc; echoes; exits asgard on failure sh "script", silent: true Same No echo sh "script", background: true Same, as a managed job Returns at once; see Background Jobs sh :name, "script" The shell registered as :name Unregistered names run from PATH with .tmp shebang ... Exactly as sh The same method under its longer name shell :name, "path", args:, ext: Class level: register a shell Executable checked at load; returns the name default_shell :name Class level: select the default Other forms register and select

The full signatures are in the DSL Reference.

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text:
A subcommand groups related tasks under one name, so you type asgard db migrate and asgard server start instead of migrate_db and start_server. Each group is its own class with its own tasks, options and help page.

The whole pattern in one file:

class DeployCommands < Tasks
  desc "Deploy to staging"
  def staging = sh "cap staging deploy"

  desc "Deploy to production"
  def production = sh "cap production deploy"
end

class Tasks
  desc "deploy SUBCOMMAND", "Deploy the application"
  subcommand "deploy", DeployCommands
end

asgard deploy staging
asgard deploy production
asgard deploy              # the group's help

The rest of this page explains what the subcommand class gets from Tasks, how dependencies and options work inside it, and how to lay out several groups across files.

docs.title: The Pattern
docs.text:
A subcommand needs two things:

  1. A class that inherits from Tasks. Its public methods with a desc are the group's tasks, exactly as in Tasks itself. The class name is yours to choose; DeployCommands, Deploy and DeployTasks all work.
  2. A registration on Tasks with subcommand "name", TheClass, preceded by a desc whose usage string is conventionally name SUBCOMMAND. The description is what asgard help shows next to the group.

The class must exist before the subcommand line runs. In a single file, write the class first. Across files, import the file that defines the class before the class Tasks body that registers it (see Across Files).

docs.title: Why Inherit from Tasks
docs.text:
Inheriting from Tasks gives the group everything a top-level task has:

  • sh and shebang, and the same shells registry and default_shell (one registry for the whole project, so a shell :bash, "/opt/homebrew/bin/bash" in .loki applies here too)
  • depends_on, scoped to the group's own tasks
  • dotenv and env
  • @@ class variables declared on Tasks, visible in every task of the group
  • The built-in --debug and --verbose options, and debug? / verbose?
  • Any class_option you added to Tasks
  • Every private helper, no_commands method and helper defined on Tasks

Two consequences of inheritance to know about:

  • The group inherits the top-level tasks as well. asgard db deploy runs the top-level deploy, and asgard db help lists the inherited tasks above the group's own, under a namespace made from the class name (asgard d_b_commands deploy). Harmless, but it is why the group's help is longer than you might expect.

  • A default_task on Tasks is inherited too. If .loki says default_task :greet, then asgard db with no further word runs greet, not the group's help. Set the group's own default:

    class DBCommands < Tasks
  default_task :help
  # ...
end

Warning

Do not redeclare class_option :debug or class_option :verbose in a subcommand class. They are inherited; declaring them again is an error.

docs.title: depends_on Within a Subcommand
docs.text:
depends_on works inside the group exactly as at the top level, and names the group's own tasks:

class DBCommands < Tasks
  desc "Run pending migrations"
  def migrate = sh "rails db:migrate"

  desc "Load seed data"
  def seed = sh "rails db:seed"

  depends_on :migrate, :seed
  desc "Migrate then seed"
  def reset = puts "Done."
end

class Tasks
  desc "db SUBCOMMAND", "Manage the database"
  subcommand "db", DBCommands
end

asgard db reset   # migrate → seed → reset

Each task still runs at most once per invocation, parallel groups still run in threads, and cycles and undefined names are still caught before anything runs. See Dependencies.

docs.title: A Complete Example: Server Commands
docs.text:
This group starts, stops and restarts a server, and remembers the port it was started on so stop and restart use the same one. It is the examples/server_subcommands.loki file from the repository:

SERVER_PORT_FILE = "tmp/.server.port".freeze

class ServerCommands < Tasks
  default_task :help     # `asgard server` shows this group's help

  # Available both in the class body and inside the tasks below
  helper(:server_port) {
    File.exist?(SERVER_PORT_FILE) ? File.read(SERVER_PORT_FILE).strip.to_i : 3000
  }

  desc "Start the server"
  option :port,    aliases: "-p", type: :numeric, default: 3000,  desc: "Port to listen on"
  option :daemon,  aliases: "-d", type: :boolean, default: false, desc: "Run as a background daemon"
  option :workers, aliases: "-w", type: :numeric, default: 2,     desc: "Number of worker processes"
  option :log,                    type: :string,  default: "log/server.log",
                                  banner: "FILE", desc: "Write logs to FILE"
  def start
    FileUtils.mkdir_p("tmp")
    File.write(SERVER_PORT_FILE, options[:port].to_s)
    puts "Starting server on :#{options[:port]} with #{options[:workers]} workers#{options[:daemon] ? ' (daemon)' : ''}..."
  end

  desc "Stop the running server"
  option :force, aliases: "-f", type: :boolean, default: false, desc: "Force-kill without draining"
  option :wait,                  type: :numeric, default: 30,   desc: "Seconds to wait for shutdown"
  def stop
    if options[:force]
      puts "Force-stopping server on :#{server_port}..."
    else
      puts "Gracefully stopping server on :#{server_port} (timeout: #{options[:wait]}s)..."
    end
  end

  desc "Show server status and process info"
  def status = puts "Server is listening on :#{server_port}"

  depends_on :stop
  desc "Restart the server on the same port it was started on"
  def restart
    puts "Starting server on :#{server_port}..."
    puts "Server restarted."
  end
end

class Tasks
  desc "server SUBCOMMAND", "Manage the application server"
  subcommand "server", ServerCommands
end

asgard server start -p 4000 --workers 4 --daemon
# Starting server on :4000 with 4 workers (daemon)...
asgard server status
# Server is listening on :4000
asgard server restart
# Gracefully stopping server on :4000 (timeout: 30s)...
# Starting server on :4000...
# Server restarted.
asgard server stop --force

Everything from Defining Tasks applies inside the group: per-task options, long_desc, map for short names, positional parameters.

docs.title: Scoped Declarations
docs.text:
Each subcommand class has its own:

Declaration Scope desc, long_desc The group's tasks method_option / option The task that follows class_option Every task in the group, in addition to the ones inherited from Tasks map Short names within the group: map "m" => "migrate" makes asgard db m work default_task What asgard db alone runs depends_on The group's own tasks

None of these leak back into Tasks or into another group.

docs.title: Several Groups
