docs.text:
Register as many as you need:

class ServerCommands < Tasks
  # ...
end

class DBCommands < Tasks
  # ...
end

class DeployCommands < Tasks
  # ...
end

class Tasks
  desc "server SUBCOMMAND", "Manage the server";   subcommand "server", ServerCommands
  desc "db SUBCOMMAND",     "Manage the database"; subcommand "db",     DBCommands
  desc "deploy SUBCOMMAND", "Deploy";              subcommand "deploy", DeployCommands
end

asgard help lists each group on one line (asgard db SUBCOMMAND # Manage the database); asgard tree adds a section per group, named after its class (d_b_commands), listing the group's own tasks.

docs.title: Subcommands Across Files
docs.text:
Give each group its own file and register them all in .loki:

myproject/
  .loki                    imports the siblings, then registers the groups
  server_subcommands.loki  defines ServerCommands
  db_subcommands.loki      defines DBCommands

# .loki
import "*.loki"

class Tasks
  desc "server SUBCOMMAND", "Manage the server";   subcommand "server", ServerCommands
  desc "db SUBCOMMAND",     "Manage the database"; subcommand "db",     DBCommands
end

The import at the top of .loki loads the siblings before .loki's own class Tasks body runs, so both classes are defined by the time the subcommand lines need them. See Task Files.

docs.title: Help for a Group
docs.text:
Three spellings reach the group's help:

asgard db            # the group's help (when the group has no default task of its own)
asgard db help       # the same
asgard help db       # the same
asgard db help migrate   # one task of the group

Commands:
  asgard db console             # Open an interactive database console
  asgard db help [COMMAND]      # Describe subcommands or one specific subcommand
  asgard db migrate [VERSION]   # Run pending migrations up to VERSION
  asgard db reset               # Rollback all migrations, re-migrate, and reseed
  ...

The inherited top-level tasks appear in the same listing under the class's namespace, as noted above.

docs.title: The Built-in Groups
docs.text: asgard schedule, asgard watcher and asgard jobs are subcommand groups too, built into asgard. They are registered under reserved names, so a task of your own called schedule, watcher or jobs does not shadow them: asgard schedule install always reaches the built-in. See Scheduled Tasks, Watched Files and Background Jobs.

docs.title: Task Files
docs.text:
Every asgard project is a directory with a file named .loki in it. That file marks the project root and is the only file asgard loads on its own. Everything else, from a second task file next to it to a library of tasks shared by a whole workspace, is something your .loki asks for with import.

This page starts with the marker itself, then covers the three ways to bring in more files (import, loki_up, import_up), the layouts that fall out of them, and what happens when two files define the same task.

The smallest possible project:

mkdir myproject && cd myproject
touch .loki
asgard help        # works; lists only asgard's built-in commands

docs.title: The .loki Root Marker
docs.text:
When you run asgard, it looks for a file named .loki in the current directory, then in its parent, and so on up to the filesystem root. The first one it finds is the project root. It is loaded, and nothing else is.

myproject/
  .loki            found from anywhere below it
  src/
    app/           asgard works from here too

Three details:

  • It may be empty. Its presence is what marks the root. A .loki with no content still lets asgard help, asgard jobs and the rest run.
  • A directory named .loki does not count. Only a file does.
  • The nearest one wins. If there is a .loki in your home directory and another in a project below it, running asgard inside the project uses the project's. The one above is never reached, and asgard --doctor lists it as a shadowed marker (see Help & Diagnostics).

Without a .loki anywhere above the current directory:

asgard: no .loki file found in /Users/you/Downloads

The three listing commands that cover every project on the machine, asgard schedule list, asgard watcher list and asgard jobs list, are the exception. They run anywhere.

docs.title: Asgard Does Not Change Directory
docs.text:
Finding .loki upward does not move you there. A task runs in the directory you ran asgard from, so a relative path in a task is relative to that directory. When a task needs the project root, ask for it:

class Tasks
  desc "Show where things are"
  def where
    puts "running in:   #{Dir.pwd}"
    puts "project root: #{loki_up.dirname}"
  end
end

cd src/app && asgard where
# running in:   /Users/you/myproject/src/app
# project root: /Users/you/myproject

Tasks started by the watcher or a schedule always run from the project root.

How asgard finds and loads task files: the .loki marker imports sibling task files, may import a shared file from a parent directory, and is found from any subdirectory.

~/sandbox/gem_tasks.loki shared by every project below it

myproject/

.loki root marker, loaded first

import_up "gem_tasks.loki"

build.loki

deploy.loki

test.loki

import "*.loki"

src/app/ $ asgard build

walks up to the nearest .loki

one Tasks class, reopened by every file asgard help lists build, deploy, test and the tasks gem_tasks.loki defines

The root .loki is found from any subdirectory. It imports its siblings, and may import a shared file from higher up. Every file reopens the same Tasks class.

docs.title: Loading Files with import
docs.text:
import loads another task file. It works at the top of a .loki file, inside a class Tasks body, and inside a task method. The usual place is the first line of .loki:

# .loki
import "*.loki"

class Tasks
  # tasks that belong at the top level, if any
end

docs.title: Every Form
docs.text:
import "build.loki"                   # one file, relative to this file's directory
import "tasks/ci.loki"                # a file in a subdirectory
import "../shared/gem_tasks.loki"     # a file in a parent directory
import "/home/shared/gem_tasks.loki"  # an absolute path
import "*.loki"                       # every .loki file beside this one
import "**/*.loki"                    # every .loki file in this directory and below
import Pathname.new("tasks.loki")     # a Pathname works too

A relative path is resolved from the directory of the file that contains the import, not from where you ran asgard. That is what makes a .loki work from any subdirectory.

docs.title: The Rules
docs.text:
• The path must end in .loki. Anything else raises ArgumentError: import: path must end with .loki. A plain Ruby file is loaded with require_relative instead (see Helper Methods).
  • A glob never matches .loki itself. *.loki picks up build.loki and deploy.loki, never the dotfile, so a .loki that imports *.loki does not load itself again.
  • Glob matches load in alphabetical order. build.loki, deploy.loki, test.loki.
  • A file loads once. Importing the same file twice, from two different files, or through both a glob and a name, loads it the first time and skips it after that. You never get a task defined twice because two files both asked for the same helper file.

  • A named file that does not exist stops asgard with a one-line error:

    asgard: /Users/you/myproject/.loki:1: cannot load such file -- /Users/you/myproject/missing.loki (LoadError)

    A glob that matches nothing is not an error; it just loads nothing.

docs.title: Return Value
docs.text:
import returns true when it loaded at least one new file and false when every match was already loaded or the glob matched nothing. You rarely need this, but it makes a conditional read naturally:

import("local_overrides.loki") || puts("no local overrides")

docs.title: Finding Files with loki_up
docs.text:
loki_up(name = ".loki") searches the current directory and each parent for a file with that name and returns its path as a Pathname, or nil. It only finds; it never loads.

Despite the name it is not limited to .loki files. Any file that lives somewhere up the tree is fair game:

loki_up                     # the .loki marker itself
loki_up("gem_tasks.loki")   # a shared task file in this directory or above
loki_up(".env")             # the nearest .env
loki_up("VERSION")          # a VERSION file

Two common uses:

class Tasks
  # Load the project's .env from any subdirectory (see Environment Variables)
  dotenv loki_up(".env") || ".env"

  # The project root, for paths that must not depend on where asgard ran
  helper(:root) { loki_up.dirname }

  desc "Build the docs"
  def docs = sh "mkdocs build -f #{root.join('mkdocs.yml')}"
end

loki_up takes an exact filename. For a pattern, use import_up.

docs.title: Loading Files Found Up the Tree with import_up
docs.text:
import_up(name = ".loki") is loki_up and import in one call: find the file in the current directory or an ancestor, then load it.

import_up "gem_tasks.loki"

Walks upward until it finds gem_tasks.loki and loads it. It returns false without raising when nothing is found, which is what makes a shared file optional:

import_up("ci_tasks.loki") || import_up("gem_tasks.loki")   # the first one found wins
import_up "team_tasks.loki"                                  # fine if it is not there

With a glob, import_up stops at the first ancestor directory that has any match and loads everything that matches there. It does not keep walking and collect matches from several levels:

~/sandbox/
  gem_tasks.loki      loaded by import_up("*.loki") from myproject/sub/
  ci_tasks.loki       also loaded: same directory as the first match
  myproject/
    .loki
    sub/              asgard runs here

Note

import_up searches from the directory you ran asgard in, not from the file that calls it. Run from myproject/sub/, a glob search looks in sub/, then myproject/, then ~/sandbox/. With an exact filename the difference rarely matters, because the file is above the project either way.

docs.title: Load Order
docs.text:
Files load in the order your .loki asks for them, and a .loki that starts with import "*.loki" loads every sibling before its own class Tasks body runs. For most things order does not matter:

  • A depends_on :build may name a task defined in a file that loads later. Dependency names are checked once every file has loaded, not when the line is read.
  • desc, options and depends_on attach to the def that follows them in the same file.

Order matters for the few things that are "first wins" or "last wins":

Declaration Rule @@name ||= value First file to set it wins; later files see the value def name Last definition wins, silently (see Task Name Overloading) default_task :name Last call wins, with a warning on stderr naming both locations header / footer Every call is kept; see Help & Diagnostics for the order they print in shell / default_shell Last call wins

When alphabetical order is not the order you want, name the files:

# .loki
import "infra.loki"     # first
import "build.loki"     # then this
import "deploy.loki"    # then this

docs.title: Tracing Imports
docs.text:
To see which files load, turn on Ruby's warnings for the run:

RUBYOPT=-w asgard build
# import: /Users/you/myproject/build.loki
# import: /Users/you/myproject/deploy.loki
# import: /Users/you/myproject/test.loki

asgard build --verbose prints the same lines, but only for an import that runs inside a task body, because the flag takes effect after the task files have loaded. Add --debug to also see a file that was skipped because it was already loaded, and an import_up that found nothing:

asgard build --verbose --debug
# import: skip /Users/you/myproject/extra.loki (already loaded)
# import_up: team_tasks.loki not found

asgard --doctor shows the whole import chain without running anything; see Help & Diagnostics.

docs.title: A Single File
docs.text:
Everything in .loki, nothing to import:

# .loki
class Tasks
  @@app ||= "myapp".freeze

  desc "Compile the project"
  def build = sh "rake build"

  desc "Run the test suite"
  def test = sh "rake test"

  desc "Build and push the gem"
  def release = sh "gem push pkg/#{@@app}-*.gem"
end

docs.title: One File per Concern
docs.text:
Split tasks by what they do and load them all with a glob:

myproject/
  .loki          imports the rest
  build.loki     compile, package
  deploy.loki    deploy to staging and production
  test.loki      tests and lint

# .loki
import "*.loki"

# build.loki
class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build = sh "rake build"
end

# test.loki
class Tasks
  depends_on :build
  desc "Run the test suite"
  def test = sh "bundle exec rake test"
end

# deploy.loki
class Tasks
  depends_on :test
  desc "Deploy to production"
  def deploy = sh "cap production deploy"
end

asgard deploy    # build → test → deploy

docs.title: A Shared Library for Many Projects
docs.text:
Put tasks that every project needs in a parent directory and let each project pull them in with import_up:

~/sandbox/
  gem_tasks.loki       build, install, release for any gem
  myproject/
    .loki
  other_project/
    .loki

# myproject/.loki
import_up "gem_tasks.loki"

class Tasks
  @@project ||= "myproject".freeze   # gem_tasks.loki reads this
end

Tip

A shared file should not hardcode the project's name. Read it from a class variable each project sets, as above, and set it with ||= so the project's value is the one that wins whichever file loads first. See Variables.

docs.title: Conditional Imports
docs.text:
A .loki is Ruby, so an import can sit inside an if:

# .loki
import "quality.loki"
import "quality_rails.loki" if ENV["RAILS_ROOT"]
import "local.loki"         if File.exist?(File.join(__dir__, "local.loki"))

The second line adds Rails-only checks when the project says it is a Rails app. A task in another file that wants "every *_check task, whichever files loaded" uses the block form of depends_on to discover them; see Dependencies.

docs.title: Subcommand Classes in Their Own Files
docs.text:
Define each subcommand class in its own file and register them in .loki. Because the siblings are imported at the top of .loki, the classes exist by the time .loki's own class Tasks body runs:

myproject/
  .loki
  db.loki
  server.loki

# db.loki
class DBCommands < Tasks
  desc "Run migrations"
  def migrate = sh "rails db:migrate"
end

# server.loki
class ServerCommands < Tasks
  desc "Start the server"
  def start = sh "rails server"
end

# .loki
import "*.loki"

class Tasks
  desc "db SUBCOMMAND",     "Manage the database"; subcommand "db",     DBCommands
  desc "server SUBCOMMAND", "Manage the server";   subcommand "server", ServerCommands
end

See Subcommands.

docs.title: Task Name Overloading
docs.text:
Every file reopens the same Tasks class, so two files can define a method with the same name. Ruby keeps the last one it sees and says nothing. The earlier task is gone: its body, its desc, and its depends_on.

# build.loki (loads first)
class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build = sh "rake build"
end

# postbuild.loki (loads second)
class Tasks
  desc "Copy assets"
  def build = sh "cp -r dist/ public/"     # this is now the only `build`
end

asgard build copies assets and never compiles. There is no error, so when a task does not do what its file says, check for a second definition. asgard --doctor reports every one:

Tasks by file:

  build.loki
    build  build.loki:3   OVERRIDDEN by postbuild.loki:3 — never callable

  postbuild.loki
    build  postbuild.loki:3   active — redefines build.loki:3

If you do mean to extend a task from another file, give each step its own task and chain them with depends_on:

class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  def build = sh "rake build"

  desc "Copy build output to public/"
  def copy_assets = sh "cp -r dist/ public/"

  depends_on :build, :copy_assets
  desc "Compile and copy assets"
  def build_all; end
end

The alias_method trick (keep the old body under a new name, then redefine) also works, but it depends on which file loads first and hides the first task from help. Prefer the version above.

docs.title: A Real Example: Asgard's Own Task Files
docs.text:
The asgard repository is run by asgard. Its root .loki is a multi-file project in exactly the shape this page describes:

# .loki
import "quality.loki"
import "quality_rails.loki" if ENV["RAILS_ROOT"]
import "gem_tasks.loki"
import "git.loki"
import "doc_tasks.loki"
import "xyzzy.loki"   # an example for the --doctor flag

class Tasks
  @@project      ||= "asgard".freeze
  @@project_desc ||= "CLI-task runner"

  watch :test_check, paths: %w[lib test], only: /\.rb\z/

  helper(:project_version) do
    @@project_version ||= File.read("lib/#{@@project}/version.rb").match(/VERSION\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/)[1].freeze
  end

  default_task :quality

  header <<~HEAD
    Project:  #{@@project} (v#{project_version}) - #{@@project_desc}
    Root Dir: #{loki_up.parent}
    Default task: #{default_task}
  HEAD
end
File What it holds quality.loki One *_check task per quality tool (tests, RuboCop, Flog, Flay, Reek, typos, ...) and a quality task whose block-form depends_on runs every *_check in parallel and prints a summary from their results quality_rails.loki Rails-only checks (Brakeman and friends), loaded only when RAILS_ROOT is set; quality picks them up with nothing else to change gem_tasks.loki console, build, install and release, each depending on quality git.loki push, pull and fetch doc_tasks.loki doc_builder and doc_server (a background job), defined only when mkdocs.yml exists xyzzy.loki A xyzzy task that .loki deliberately redefines, so asgard --doctor has an override to report

Clone the repository and run asgard help, asgard tree and asgard --doctor from its root to see each of these in action. The Examples page walks through the rest of examples/.

docs.title: Summary of Loading Rules
docs.text: Call Finds? Loads? Glob? Searches ancestors? Not found loki_up(name) Yes, returns a Pathname No No Yes Returns nil import(path) No Yes Yes No Named file: error; glob: nothing loads import_up(name) Yes Yes Yes, first matching ancestor Yes Returns false Starting asgard .loki only .loki only No Yes asgard: no .loki file found in ...

docs.title: Defining Tasks
docs.text: A task is a public method inside class Tasks with a desc line above it. That is the whole rule. This page starts there and then adds, one step at a time, everything a task can have: parameters, typed options, extended help, hidden tasks, a default, short aliases, and control over the exit status. Asgard is built on Thor, so Thor's own words (desc, method_option, long_desc, map, default_task, argument) are the ones you write.

docs.title: Basic Task
docs.text:
class Tasks
  desc "Say hello"
  def hello = puts "Hello, World!"
end

asgard hello

Hello, World!

The method body can be any Ruby. A one-line method reads well with the def name = expression form; a longer one uses the usual def ... end.

docs.title: Describing a Task: desc
docs.text:
desc takes one or two strings.

With one, it is the description shown by asgard help, and the usage line is the method name:

desc "Run the test suite"
def test = sh "bundle exec rake test"

asgard test  # Run the test suite

With two, the first is the usage line and the second the description. Use the two-argument form whenever the task takes something after its name, so the help says so:

desc "greet NAME", "Greet NAME by name"
def greet(name = "World") = puts "Hello, #{name}!"

asgard greet NAME  # Greet NAME by name

desc goes directly above the def. depends_on (see Dependencies) goes above the def too, in either order with desc.

The description is one line, shown in the command list. For a longer explanation that asgard help TASK prints under the usage and options, add long_desc; see Extended Help: long_desc below. To describe a task but keep it out of the list, add hide: true; see Hidden Tasks.

docs.title: Positional Parameters
docs.text:
A task's positional parameters are its method's parameters. Give each a default so the task also runs with nothing after its name:

class Tasks
  desc "greet NAME", "Greet NAME; omit NAME to greet the world"
  def greet(name = "World")
    puts "Hello, #{name}!"
  end

  desc "copy FROM TO", "Copy FROM to TO"
  def copy(from, to) = sh "cp #{from} #{to}"
end

asgard greet            # Hello, World!
asgard greet Alice      # Hello, Alice!
asgard copy a.txt b.txt
asgard copy a.txt

ERROR: "asgard copy" was called with arguments ["a.txt"]
Usage: "asgard copy FROM TO"

A missing required parameter is a usage error: the message prints and asgard exits 1.

Dependencies cannot take required parameters

A task that another task lists in depends_on is run with no arguments. If it has a required parameter, asgard refuses at startup: asgard: task 'copy' has 2 required argument(s) and cannot be used as a dependency. Give the parameter a default, or read the value from an option or an environment variable instead.

A splat collects everything that follows:

desc "lint FILES...", "Lint the given files (default: lib)"
def lint(*files)
  files = ["lib"] if files.empty?
  sh "rubocop #{files.join(' ')}"
end

docs.title: Named Options
docs.text:
option (or its longer name method_option) declares a flag for the task that follows it. Inside the task, options.name or options[:name] holds the value, and a boolean reads as options.name?.

class Tasks
  desc "Compile the project"
  option :output,  aliases: "-o", type: :string,  default: "dist/", desc: "Output directory"
  option :verbose, aliases: "-v", type: :boolean, default: false,   desc: "Enable verbose output"
  option :jobs,    aliases: "-j", type: :numeric, default: 1,       desc: "Number of parallel jobs"
  option :tags,                   type: :array,                     desc: "Build tags to apply"
  option :defines,                type: :hash,                      desc: "Preprocessor defines (KEY:VALUE)"
  def compile
    puts "Compiling into #{options.output} with #{options.jobs} job(s)"
    puts "Tags: #{options.tags.join(', ')}" if options.tags
    puts "Defines: #{options.defines}"      if options.defines
    puts "(verbose)"                        if options.verbose?
  end
end

asgard compile -o build/ -j 4 --tags debug release --defines VERSION:2 MODE:fast

Compiling into build/ with 4 job(s)
Tags: debug, release
Defines: {"VERSION"=>"2", "MODE"=>"fast"}

docs.title: Reading an Option
docs.text:
options answers three spellings, all the same value:

Spelling Returns options.jobs The value, or nil when the option was not given and has no default options[:jobs] The same; a string key, options["jobs"], works too options.verbose? true or false, never nil; the natural form for a boolean

A predicate with an argument compares: options.format?("md") is options[:format] == "md".

docs.title: The Five Option Types
docs.text:
Type On the command line Value in the task :string --output dist/ or --output=dist/ "dist/" :boolean --verbose / --no-verbose true / false :numeric --jobs 4 4 :array --tags foo bar baz ["foo", "bar", "baz"] :hash --defines KEY:val FOO:bar {"KEY"=>"val", "FOO"=>"bar"}

An option with no type: is a string. Every boolean also accepts its --no- form, and --skip-name means the same as --no-name.

docs.title: Option Keys
docs.text: Key Meaning aliases A short form, "-o", or several, %w[-o --out] type One of the five types above default The value when the flag is not given required true makes omitting the flag a usage error desc The one-line description shown in help enum The allowed values; anything else is a usage error banner The placeholder shown in help for the value, instead of the type name

docs.title: A Required Option
docs.text:
class Tasks
  desc "deploy ENV", "Deploy to ENV"
  option :strategy, type: :string, required: true, enum: %w[blue-green rolling canary], desc: "Deployment strategy"
  def deploy(env = "staging")
    sh "cap #{env} deploy --strategy #{options[:strategy]}"
  end
end

asgard deploy

No value provided for required options '--strategy'

asgard deploy --strategy rolling
asgard deploy production --strategy blue-green

docs.title: Validating with enum
docs.text:
class Tasks
  desc "Build the project"
  option :env, type: :string, default: "development", enum: %w[development staging production], desc: "Target environment"
  def build = sh "rake build ENV=#{options[:env]}"
end

asgard build --env prod

Expected '--env' to be one of development, staging, production; got prod

docs.title: A Clearer Placeholder with banner
docs.text:
class Tasks
  desc "Wait for a service to come up"
  option :timeout, type: :numeric, default: 30, banner: "SECONDS", desc: "Give up after SECONDS"
  def wait = sh "wait-for-it localhost:3000 --timeout #{options[:timeout]}"
end

asgard help wait shows [--timeout=SECONDS] instead of [--timeout=N].

Options that every task should accept are declared once with class_option; see Options & Flags.

docs.title: Extended Help: long_desc
docs.text:
long_desc adds a longer explanation that asgard help <task> prints after the usage and options. The text is re-wrapped to the terminal width; put \x5 at the end of a line to force a line break there, which keeps example commands on their own lines:

class Tasks
  long_desc <<~DESC
    Generates a project report covering test coverage, lint results,
    and a dependency audit.

    Pass --format to control the output style. Use --since to limit the
    report to changes after a given date.

    Examples:\x5
      asgard report --format html --since 2024-01-01\x5
      asgard report --format json --output report.json\x5
      asgard report --format text
  DESC
  desc "Generate a project report"
  option :format, type: :string, default: "text", enum: %w[text html json], desc: "Output format"
  option :since,  type: :string, banner: "DATE",                            desc: "Limit to changes after DATE"
  option :output, type: :string, banner: "FILE",                            desc: "Write the report to FILE"
  def report = sh "generate-report --format #{options[:format]}"
end

asgard help report

Usage:
  asgard report

Options:
  [--format=FORMAT]  # Output format
                     # Default: text
                     # Possible values: text, html, json
  [--since=DATE]     # Limit to changes after DATE
  [--output=FILE]    # Write the report to FILE
  ...

Description:
  Generates a project report covering test coverage, lint results, and a
  dependency audit.

  Pass --format to control the output style. Use --since to limit the report
  to changes after a given date.

  Examples:
    asgard report --format html --since 2024-01-01
    asgard report --format json --output report.json
    asgard report --format text

long_desc, desc, the options and depends_on can appear in any order; they all apply to the next def.

docs.title: Hidden Tasks
docs.text:
A hidden task runs from the command line and can be a dependency, but asgard help leaves it out. There are two ways to get one.

Ask for it with hide: true. Use this for a task that is part of the project's machinery and not something a person would type:

class Tasks
  desc "Ask before running the task that depends on this", hide: true
  def confirm
    answer = ask("Really run `asgard #{ARGV.join(' ')}`? [y/N]")
    raise Asgard::Error, "aborted" unless answer.strip.downcase.start_with?("y")
  end

  depends_on :confirm
  desc "Drop and recreate the database"
  def reset_database = sh "bin/rails db:reset"
end

asgard help shows reset_database but not confirm; asgard confirm still works.

Leave out the desc. A public method with no desc is also a hidden task:

class Tasks
  def current_sha = `git rev-parse --short HEAD`.strip   # a hidden task, by accident
end

asgard current_sha      # runs, prints nothing, exits 0

Helpers must not be public methods

This catches people who write helper methods as plain defs. Every public method is a task: asgard current_sha runs it, depends_on :current_sha accepts it, and asgard --doctor lists it as hidden (no desc; not shown by help). Make helpers private, put them inside no_commands do ... end, or define them with helper. All three are on Helper Methods.

docs.title: Default Task
docs.text:
default_task names the task that runs when you type asgard with nothing after it:

class Tasks
  default_task :greet

  desc "Say hello (runs by default)"
  def greet = puts "Hello from Asgard!"
end

asgard            # same as: asgard greet

Without default_task, a bare asgard prints the help.

Only one default can win. When a second file sets another, asgard warns on standard error and the last one loaded is used:

asgard: default_task :deploy at /proj/deploy.loki:3 overrides default_task :greet set at /proj/.loki:2

docs.title: Abbreviated Command Matching
docs.text:
Every task is a Thor command, and Thor resolves any unambiguous prefix of a command name to that command automatically. Nothing to declare. Given:

class Tasks
  desc "Check code style with RuboCop"
  def rubocop_check = sh "bundle exec rubocop"

  desc "Run the test suite"
  def test_check = sh "bundle exec rake test"

  desc "Run the test suite with verbose output"
  def test_verbose = sh "bundle exec rake test -v"

  desc "Deploy to production"
  def deploy = sh "cap production deploy"

  desc "Deploy to staging"
  def deploy_staging = sh "cap staging deploy"
end

asgard r             # same as: asgard rubocop_check, the only task starting with "r"
asgard test_c        # same as: asgard test_check, enough of the name to be unique
asgard test          # Ambiguous command test matches [test_check, test_verbose]
asgard deploy        # runs deploy, not deploy_staging; see below

Matching is on a plain prefix, so the shortest string that is still unique among your tasks works. Two details worth knowing:

  • An exact full name always wins, even if it is also a prefix of another task. asgard deploy runs deploy itself, never the ambiguous-prefix error, because deploy is a defined command and not merely a prefix of deploy_staging.
  • An ambiguous prefix produces a clean error listing every candidate (Ambiguous command X matches [...]) rather than guessing or running the first match. Type enough of the name to disambiguate.

Tip

Because matching depends on every task name currently defined, a short prefix that is unique today can become ambiguous tomorrow when a new task with the same stem is added. Adding rubocop_fix alongside rubocop_check turns asgard r from a clean match into Ambiguous command r matches [rubocop_check, rubocop_fix]. Use map for a short name that must stay stable.

docs.title: Command Aliases
docs.text:
map gives a task another name. Several aliases can point at one task:

class Tasks
  map "t"   => "test"
  map "b"   => "build"
  map "-v"  => "version"

  desc "Print the project version"
  def version = puts "1.4.0"

  desc "Run tests"
  def test = sh "bundle exec rake test"

  desc "Build the gem"
  def build = sh "gem build myapp.gemspec"
end

asgard t       # same as: asgard test
asgard b       # same as: asgard build
asgard -v      # same as: asgard version (asgard's own flag is --version)

An alias does not appear in asgard help; the task it points at does.

docs.title: Return Values and Exit Status
docs.text:
What a task returns decides asgard's exit status, which is what a shell script or CI job sees.

The task Exit status Returns :fail 1 Returns anything else (nil, true, :warn, :skip, a string) 0 Raises Asgard::Error, "message" 1, after printing asgard: message Runs an sh command that fails The command's exit status; asgard stops at that command Calls abort "message" 1, after printing the message

The :fail convention suits a check that reports its own result and should not stop other work:

class Tasks
  desc "Check code style with RuboCop"
  def rubocop_check
    output = `bundle exec rubocop 2>&1`
    File.write("rubocop_output.txt", output)
    puts "RuboCop: #{output.lines.find { |l| l.include?('files inspected') }&.strip} (see rubocop_output.txt)"
    $?.success? ? :pass : :fail
  end
end

asgard rubocop_check; echo "exit: $?"

RuboCop: 12 files inspected, 3 offenses detected (see rubocop_output.txt)
exit: 1

raise Asgard::Error is for a task that must stop everything with a message and no backtrace:

desc "Release the gem"
def release
  raise Asgard::Error, "working tree is not clean" unless `git status --porcelain`.empty?
  sh "gem push pkg/myapp.gem"
end

asgard: working tree is not clean

Note

A dependency's return value never stops the task that depends on it: if rubocop_check returns :fail as a dependency of build, build still runs. To stop a chain, raise Asgard::Error or let a failing sh exit. How dependencies report failure is covered on Dependencies.

docs.title: Reserved Names
docs.text:
Some names belong to the machinery that runs your tasks, and a task or helper by one of them would break every command. Asgard refuses them when the .loki loads, naming the file and line:

class Tasks
  desc "Run everything"
  def run = sh "make all"
end

asgard: 'run' at /proj/.loki:3 is a name Thor reserves and cannot be a task or helper; rename it

The reserved names are the ones Thor uses internally, among them run, shell, options, invoke, args, action, behavior, root, inside, in_root, create_file, add_file and run_ruby_script. Pick another word (run_all, start) or put the task in a subcommand.

Names starting with _ are asgard's own. Asgard's built-in commands use them, and asgard _anything is refused with asgard: unknown command '_anything'. Do not start a task or helper name with an underscore.

docs.title: Formal Argument Declaration
docs.text:
argument declares a positional parameter with metadata: a type, a default, allowed values and a description that shows in help.

Class-level scope

argument applies to every task in the class, not just the one that follows it. It suits a single-command tool, or a class whose tasks all take the same first value. In a .loki with many tasks, use method parameters instead.

class Tasks
  argument :name, type: :string, default: "World", desc: "Name to greet"

  desc "hello NAME", "Say hello to NAME"
  def hello = puts "Hello, #{name}!"
end

For a multi-task file, the same thing as a method parameter:

def hello(name = "World") = puts "Hello, #{name}!"

docs.title: Running Several Tasks in One Command
docs.text: asgard runs one task per invocation, plus its dependencies. The do task in the repository's examples adds the asgard do lint test build style on top, as an ordinary task you can copy into your own .loki; steps can carry their own arguments when separated by commas. See Examples.

docs.title: Helpers
docs.text: Not every method should be a task. private methods, no_commands blocks and the helper DSL all define methods your tasks can call that never show up as commands. They are covered on Helper Methods.

docs.title: Upgrading to 0.6.0
docs.text:
Version 0.6.0 changes how asgard names a project on disk. Every scheduled task and every watcher installed by an earlier version is filed under the old name, and asgard 0.6.0 does not migrate them. If you use schedule or watch, follow the steps on this page: stop everything under the old version, upgrade, then start everything again.

sh and shebang changed too, and two of those changes can break a .loki: the exec: keyword is gone, and every sh script now runs under bash, which must be on PATH. Both are covered at the end of this page, starting at sh and shebang: exec: removed. The other changes in the release are listed in the Changelog.

docs.title: What Changed
docs.text:
Each project's scheduled jobs and watcher state are kept outside the repository, under a name derived from the project. Before 0.6.0 that name was the basename of the directory holding .loki, slugified: a project at ~/work/api was simply api.

Before 0.6.0 From 0.6.0 Project slug api api-9f3a1c2b launchd label com.madbomber.asgard.api.<name> com.madbomber.asgard.api-9f3a1c2b.<name> systemd units asgard.api.<name>.{service,timer} asgard.api-9f3a1c2b.<name>.{service,timer} Watcher state ~/.local/state/asgard/watch/api/ ~/.local/state/asgard/watch/api-9f3a1c2b/

The suffix is the CRC32 of the project's full real path, written as eight hex digits. It is stable for as long as the project stays where it is, and it is the same whether you reach the project through a symlink or not.

docs.title: Why It Was Necessary
docs.text:
A directory name is not unique on a machine. Two checkouts called api, a repository and its examples/ directory alongside another repository's examples/, a fork next to its upstream: any of these gave two projects the same slug, and the slug was the only thing that told them apart.

The consequences were silent:

  • asgard schedule install in one project removed the other's jobs. Install prunes every installed entry under the project's slug that the current .loki no longer declares. With a shared slug, the other project's entries looked like entries of this project that had been removed from .loki, so they were uninstalled.
  • The two watchers fought over one state directory. Both wrote their root into the same root file, both used the same pidfile, so starting the second watcher was refused because "the watcher is already running", and watcher list showed one project's entries under the other's name.

Hashing the full path into the slug makes every project's name unique without making it unreadable: the basename still comes first, and asgard schedule list --all and asgard watcher list --all show the full path next to each slug.

docs.title: Before You Upgrade
docs.text:
Do this with the old version still installed, so its commands find the entries under their old names.

1. Find every project with schedules or watches. Both commands work from any directory:

asgard schedule list --all
asgard watcher list --all

Each group is titled Project: <slug> (<path>). The path is where to go next.

2. In each of those projects, remove the schedules and stop the watcher:

cd /path/to/project
asgard schedule remove      # unloads and deletes every job of this project
asgard watcher stop         # a task already running finishes first

schedule remove prints one removed <name> line per entry. watcher stop waits for any running task, then prints stopped watcher for <slug>.

3. Check that nothing is left:

asgard schedule list --all   # No scheduled tasks installed
asgard watcher list --all    # every project shows DAEMON stopped

Note

A watcher that shows as stopped may still own a state directory under ~/.local/state/asgard/watch/<old slug>/. It holds only the log and the last-run records and is harmless, but you can delete it once the watcher is stopped if you want a clean slate.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
gem update asgard
asgard --version     # 0.6.0

docs.title: After You Upgrade
docs.text:
In each project, install the schedules and start the watcher again. The declarations in .loki are unchanged; only the name they are filed under is new.

cd /path/to/project
asgard schedule install
asgard watcher start

Confirm the new slugs:

asgard schedule list --all
asgard watcher list --all

Every project title now ends in a hash, for example Project: api-9f3a1c2b (/Users/you/work/api).

docs.title: If You Already Upgraded
docs.text:
Entries installed by the old version are still there and still run. The new version sees them as belonging to another project, because their slug has no hash, so they appear in schedule list --all and watcher list --all under the old name while your project's own entries, once reinstalled, appear under the new one.

Scheduled tasks. A leftover entry can be stopped by its old slug:

asgard schedule stop api/nightly      # the old slug was the bare basename

Stopping disables the job but leaves its files. To remove them, delete the job by hand:

macOS (launchd)Linux (systemd) 
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.madbomber.asgard.api.nightly
rm ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.madbomber.asgard.api.nightly.plist

systemctl --user disable --now asgard.api.nightly.timer
rm ~/.config/systemd/user/asgard.api.nightly.{service,timer}
systemctl --user daemon-reload

Watchers. A leftover daemon keeps running under the old slug. Its pidfile names it:

kill $(cat ~/.local/state/asgard/watch/api/watcher.pid)
rm -r ~/.local/state/asgard/watch/api

The daemon handles TERM the same way watcher stop does: it stops listening, lets a running task finish, and exits.

Then install and start under the new version as described above.

docs.title: Related Changes in 0.6.0
docs.text:
Two smaller changes came with the slug and are worth knowing:

  • In a project/name argument to schedule stop, start, trigger or log, the project may be the whole slug or just the directory name when that is enough to pick one project out: asgard schedule stop api/nightly reaches api-9f3a1c2b/nightly.
  • schedule list --all and watcher list --all mark a project whose directory no longer exists with [root missing]. Its jobs were left behind by a move or a delete, and the hash will not match the project at its new location, so remove them the same way as the leftovers above and reinstall from the new location.

docs.title: sh and shebang: exec: removed
docs.text:
sh and shebang no longer take an exec: keyword. sh is shebang with the default shell, so this is one change, not two. A .loki that still passes it fails on the first call:

ArgumentError: unknown keyword: :exec

What to do: delete the keyword. The task keeps working the same way.

# before
def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve", exec: true

# from 0.6.0
def doc_server = sh "mkdocs serve"

Why it was removed. exec: true promised to replace the asgard process with the command, so that nothing idle sat in memory beside a dev server and a signal sent to the pid reached the command directly. Since 0.6.0 every script runs as a file under its shell, and a shell does not hand its pid to the last command of a script file. With exec: true the pid was bash, the command was its child, and a kill of that pid stopped bash and left the command running on its own. The keyword no longer did what the documentation said.

Without it, the shell is the unit of work: when the script finishes the shell exits, asgard exits with its status, and Ctrl-C reaches asgard, the shell and the command together because they share the terminal's process group. That is the behaviour exec: true was meant to give, and it is now the only behaviour.

docs.title: sh and shebang: every script runs under bash
docs.text: Before 0.6.0 a one-line sh "..." went through Ruby's system, which hands a single string to /bin/sh, while a multi-line script went through bash. The same sh call therefore ran under two different shells depending on line count, and bash syntax passed or failed with it. From 0.6.0 sh is shebang :bash: one line or many is written to a tempfile and run by the :bash entry of the shells registry. Three things follow.

docs.title: bash must be on PATH
docs.text:
The seeded :bash entry is the bare word bash, found on PATH at run time. A machine or container with only /bin/sh fails on the first sh:

asgard: shell :bash not found: bash ...

and asgard exits 127. Every desktop system, and any image that installs bash, is unaffected.

What to do, if you cannot install bash:

class Tasks
  default_shell :sh           # sh and a nameless shebang run /bin/sh's `sh`
end

or keep :bash as the name and point it somewhere else:

class Tasks
  shell :bash, "/bin/sh"      # every sh and shebang :bash runs this instead
end

The first form is right when your scripts are POSIX sh already. The second is a quick way to get a container running; scripts that use bash features will then fail under /bin/sh the way they did before 0.6.0.

docs.title: One-liners now run under bash, not /bin/sh
docs.text:
On macOS /bin/sh is bash in POSIX mode, so one-liners behave almost exactly as before. On Debian and Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash, so a one-line script that ran under dash now runs under bash. Bash accepts nearly everything dash does, so this mostly adds features rather than removing them, but a few builtins differ:

dash (/bin/sh on Debian) bash echo "a\tb" interprets \t prints \t literally (use printf) [ a == b ] error: unexpected operator works

What to do: nothing, unless a one-liner depended on dash-only behaviour. A script that needs /bin/sh exactly can ask for it by name: shebang :sh, "...". The :sh entry is seeded and runs sh from PATH.

docs.title: $0 is a tempfile path
docs.text:
A script that printed $0, typically in a usage message, used to show bash or the command itself. It now shows the tempfile the script was written to, such as /var/folders/.../T/asgard_20261024-80545-bmbloc.sh. The file is deleted when the script finishes.

What to do: print a name you choose instead of $0. Nothing else reads it.

docs.title: Also changed, not breaking
docs.text:
• sh and shebang return true; they used to return nil.
  • A command that ends on a signal exits 128 plus the signal number, as a shell would. It used to raise a TypeError from a nil exit status.
  • A missing interpreter is named in the error message and exits 127 instead of exiting 127 silently.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
A .loki file is plain Ruby, so the values your tasks share, an application name, a port, a build directory, are plain Ruby variables. One kind of variable is the right one for a task file, and this page explains which and why, with enough Ruby for a reader who has never written any.

The short version: declare shared values as @@name at the top of class Tasks, with ||= and .freeze:

class Tasks
  @@app  ||= "myapp".freeze
  @@port ||= 3000

  desc "Print app info"
  def info = puts "#{@@app} on port #{@@port}"
end

asgard info
# myapp on port 3000

docs.title: Ruby Variable Kinds
docs.text:
Ruby has four kinds of variable plus constants, each with its own prefix and its own scope. Tasks are methods, so the wrong kind is simply invisible where you expect it:

Kind Prefix Example Visible in Local none count = 0 The method or block it is set in Instance @ @sha = "abc" One object; inside a task, that task run Class @@ @@app = "myapp" The class body, every task, every subcommand Global $ $DEBUG = true The whole process Constant Capital letter APP = "myapp" Everywhere

docs.title: Local Variables
docs.text:
A local variable lives in the method it is set in and disappears when the method returns:

def build
  output_dir = "dist"            # only this method can see it
  sh "rake build OUTDIR=#{output_dir}"
end

No other task can see output_dir. Locals are for values a single task computes and uses.

docs.title: Instance Variables (@)
docs.text:
Inside a task, @name belongs to the object running that task. It is handy for caching a value within one run:

def version
  @version ||= `git describe --tags`.strip   # computed once per run, then reused
end

In the class body, outside any method, @name sets a variable on the class itself, which is a different object from the one that runs tasks. So this does not work:

class Tasks
  @app = "myapp"         # on the class, not on the task runner

  def build
    puts @app            # nil
  end
end

Two more cautions. An instance variable set by one task is visible to a later task in the same run only when they run one after another; tasks in a parallel depends_on group each get their own object, so pass values with dep_result instead (see Dependencies). And a value that should be shared belongs in @@, below.

docs.title: Class Variables (@@)
docs.text:
@@name is shared by the class body, every task method and every subclass, which includes subcommand classes. That is exactly the set of places a task file's configuration needs to reach, so @@ is the kind to use:

class Tasks
  @@app = "myapp"        # visible in every task and every subcommand

  def build
    puts @@app           # "myapp"
  end
end

docs.title: Global Variables ($)
docs.text: $name is visible everywhere in the process, including inside every gem asgard loads. Asgard itself uses two: --debug sets $DEBUG and --verbose sets $VERBOSE, which you read with debug? and verbose? (see Options & Flags). $stdout and $stderr are the output streams puts and warn write to. Avoid declaring your own globals; @@ does the job without leaking into everything else.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
A name that starts with a capital letter is a constant. Constants are visible everywhere, with no prefix, inside and outside the class:

APP_NAME = "myapp".freeze
BASE_URL = "https://example.com".freeze

class Tasks
  desc "Deploy the app"
  def deploy
    puts "Deploying #{APP_NAME} to #{BASE_URL}"
    sh "cap deploy"
  end
end

Ruby warns when a constant is assigned twice but does not prevent it, which matters when two .loki files both define APP_NAME. Use .freeze so the value itself cannot be changed.

Constant @@ class variable Visible in tasks and subcommands Yes Yes Visible outside Tasks Yes No Second assignment Warning Silent (so use \|\|=) Convention ALL_CAPS snake_case

Constants suit values that never change: an application name, a URL, a port. @@ with ||= suits values a later file might want to set first or override.

docs.title: The Pattern
docs.text:
class Tasks
  @@app  ||= "myapp".freeze
  @@port ||= 3000
  @@env  ||= "production".freeze
end

Why ||= and not =? Every .loki file reopens the same class Tasks. With ||=, the first file to set a value wins and a later file that reopens the class does not overwrite it. That lets a shared task library ship a default that a project's own .loki sets first.

Why .freeze? It makes the value itself unchangeable, so @@app << "-extra" raises an error instead of quietly altering a name every task uses. Numbers and symbols are already frozen; freeze strings, arrays and hashes.

Why @@ and not @? A single @ in the class body is not visible inside task methods, as shown above. @@ is visible everywhere a task file needs.

docs.title: Use Double Quotes
docs.text:
Ruby has single and double quoted strings. Task files use double quotes throughout, because only double quotes support interpolation, and shell commands almost always need a value embedded:

@@app ||= "myapp".freeze
sh "bundle exec rake test"

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
#{...} inside a double-quoted string inserts the value of any Ruby expression:

class Tasks
  @@app ||= "myapp".freeze
  @@env ||= "production".freeze

  desc "Deploy the app"
  def deploy = sh "cap #{@@env} deploy APP=#{@@app}"
end

Any expression works, not just a variable name:

puts "build started at #{Time.now}"
sh "puma -p #{env(:port, '3000').to_i + 1}"
sh "git tag #{@@app}-#{`git describe --tags`.strip}"

docs.title: Multi-line Scripts
docs.text:
For a script with several lines, use a heredoc. <<~ strips the leading indentation so the script lines up with your Ruby, and interpolation works inside it:

desc "Bootstrap the project"
def bootstrap
  sh <<~SHELL
    bundle install
    rails db:create db:migrate
    echo "#{@@app} ready on #{env(:port, '3000')}"
  SHELL
end

The word after <<~ (here SHELL) is any marker you like; the heredoc ends at a line holding only that marker. See Shell Commands for what happens when the script runs.

docs.title: Sharing Values Across Files
docs.text:
All .loki files reopen one Tasks class, so a @@ variable set in one file is visible in every file loaded in the same run:

# config.loki
class Tasks
  @@app  ||= "myapp".freeze
  @@port ||= 8080
end

# deploy.loki
class Tasks
  desc "Deploy the app"
  def deploy = sh "cap deploy APP=#{@@app} PORT=#{@@port}"
end

The file that sets the value must load before the task that reads it runs, which is always true: every file loads before any task runs. Only the class body itself runs at load time, so a header line that interpolates @@app must come after the file that sets it has been imported. See Task Files for load order.

docs.title: Sharing Values With Subcommands
docs.text:
Subcommand classes inherit from Tasks, so they see its @@ variables:

# config.loki
class Tasks
  @@app ||= "myapp".freeze
end

# deploy.loki
class DeployCommands < Tasks
  desc "Deploy to production"
  def production = sh "cap production deploy APP=#{@@app}"    # visible here
end

class Tasks
  desc "deploy SUBCOMMAND", "Deployment tasks"
  subcommand "deploy", DeployCommands
end

docs.title: Computed Values
docs.text:
A value that comes from a command, a file or any other runtime computation is a method, not a variable. Make it private so it is not a task:

class Tasks
  desc "Show version info"
  def info = puts "#{version} (#{sha})"

  private

  def version = `git describe --tags`.strip
  def sha     = `git rev-parse --short HEAD`.strip
end

Warning

A public method without a desc is a hidden task: it runs from the command line and can be a dependency, it is just left out of asgard help. Helpers must be private, inside a no_commands block, or defined with helper. See Helper Methods.

Cache an expensive value with @name ||= inside the method, so it is computed once per run:

def version
  @version ||= `git describe --tags`.strip
end

When the value is also needed in the class body, in a header line for instance, define it with helper, which makes it available in both places at once:

class Tasks
  @@project ||= "myapp".freeze

  helper(:version) { File.read("lib/myapp/version.rb")[/VERSION\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/, 1] }

  header "#{@@project} v#{version}"       # class body

  desc "Show the current version"
  def show_version = puts version          # task body
end

Helper Methods has the details.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Values that come from outside the task file, from the shell, CI or a .env file, are read with env, which upcases the name and takes a default:

class Tasks
  dotenv                                   # load .env, if there is one

  desc "Start the server"
  def start = sh "puma -p #{env(:port, '3000')}"     # "3000" when PORT is unset

  desc "Deploy the app"
  def deploy = sh "cap #{env(:deploy_target)} deploy"  # error when DEPLOY_TARGET is unset
end

Environment values are always strings; convert with .to_i or compare with == "true". The whole story, including dotenv, .env files and the variables asgard itself sets, is on the Environment Variables page.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Class variables use snake_case, words separated by underscores:

class Tasks
  @@app_name    ||= "myapp".freeze
  @@deploy_host ||= "production.example.com".freeze
  @@max_workers ||= 4
end

Names to avoid

Methods and variables share a namespace with the words asgard and Thor use internally. Do not name a method shell, options, invoke, run, args or any other name on that list; a .loki that does is refused at load time with the file and line. The list is in Defining Tasks. @@options or @@shell as variables are legal but confusing next to the options and shell methods, so pick something more specific.

docs.title: Watched Files
docs.text:
Any task can run whenever files change. You say which files in the project's .loki with a watch line, and asgard watcher start runs one background process for the project that listens for changes and runs the matching tasks. Each run is a normal asgard <task>, started from the project root, and the task can ask what changed through changes.

Watching is built in. There is nothing to install or require beyond asgard itself.

docs.title: The Shortest Example
docs.text:
# .loki
class Tasks
  desc "Run the test suite"
  def test = sh "bundle exec rake test"

  watch :test, paths: %w[lib test], only: /\.rb\z/
end

asgard watcher start

started watcher for api-9f3a1c2b (pid 12345); log: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/watch/api-9f3a1c2b/watcher.log

Now edit a Ruby file under lib/ or test/ and look at the log:

echo "# tweak" >> lib/api.rb
asgard watcher log

2026-10-24 09:12:01 trigger test task=test lib/api.rb
2026-10-24 09:12:01 spawn test task=test pid=12351 lib/api.rb
bundle exec rake test
Run options: --seed 4211
...
2026-10-24 09:12:04 exit test task=test pid=12351 status=0 seconds=3.10

The watcher keeps running after you close the terminal. asgard watcher stop ends it.

Saved files reach the watcher daemon, which queues one run per task and starts each as its own asgard process; every task's output lands in watcher.log, and asgard watcher stop ends the daemon.

files you save lib/greeter.rb docs/index.md

watcher daemon one per project, matches each change against the watch declarations queue for lint: one run at a time queue for docs: one run at a time

asgard lint changes.modified = ["lib/greeter.rb"]

asgard docs changes.modified = ["docs/index.md"]

watcher.log trigger, spawn, task output, exit

asgard watcher stop running tasks finish first

output different tasks run at the same time; a task never overlaps itself

Saved files reach the watcher, which queues one run per task and starts each run as its own asgard process. Every task's output lands in watcher.log.

docs.title: Declaring Watches
docs.text:
watch goes at class level inside Tasks. Each line names a task and the paths it cares about.

class Tasks
  watch :lint,    paths: "lib/**/*.rb"
  watch :test,    paths: %w[lib test], only: /\.rb\z/, ignore: %r{\Afixtures/}
  watch :docs,    paths: "docs", env: { BUILD_ENV: "dev" }
  watch :reindex, paths: "data/**/*.json", events: %i[added removed], debounce: 1
  watch :gems,    paths: "Gemfile.lock"
  watch :lint,    paths: "bin/**/*", as: "lint-bin"
end
Keyword Meaning paths: A directory, a file or a glob, relative to the project root, or an Array of them only: A Regexp, or an Array of them, that a changed path must match (matched against the path relative to the watched directory) ignore: A Regexp, or an Array of them, that silences a path; added to the default ignores events: Which kinds of change count: :all (the default), :changed, :added, :removed, or an Array of them; :modified is accepted as another name for :changed debounce: Seconds to wait after the last change before the task runs (default 0.5) env: { KEY: "value" }: environment variables added to the task's process as: The entry's name (see Entry Names)

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
A path is one of three things, judged in the project root:

You write What is watched "docs" (an existing directory) Everything beneath it, at any depth "Gemfile.lock" (a file, or a name with an extension) Just that file; it may not exist yet "lib/**/*.rb" (a glob) The directory before the first wildcard, keeping only paths that match

Globs follow shell rules: ** spans directories, * and ? stay within one path segment, and {a,b} is an alternative:

watch :assets, paths: "app/assets/**/*.{js,css}"
watch :notes,  paths: "notes/*.md"            # only the top level of notes/

Paths must be relative. An absolute path, or no path at all, is rejected when the .loki loads: watch :lint paths are relative to the project root (got "/tmp/x").

docs.title: Mixing Directories and Patterns
docs.text:
A bare directory cannot share a declaration with a pattern or a file. The filter a pattern creates would apply to the directory as well, and silently drop most of what you meant to watch, so asgard refuses the combination:

asgard: /proj/.loki:4: watch :build mixes a bare directory with patterns or files, which would filter the directory too; declare them separately or write the directory as dir/**/* (ArgumentError)

Either fix works:

watch :build, paths: %w[src/**/* config/*.yml]     # the directory as a glob
# or
watch :build, paths: "src"
watch :build, paths: "config/*.yml", as: "build-config"

docs.title: Narrowing with only:
docs.text:
only: adds a filter on top of the paths. A path must match one of the patterns from paths: and one of the only: expressions. The filter is applied to every directory the declaration watches, so with paths: %w[lib/**/*.rb docs/**/*.md] a .md file under lib/ also matches; use separate declarations when that matters.

watch :test, paths: %w[lib test], only: /\.rb\z/
watch :docs, paths: "docs", only: [/\.md\z/, /\.yml\z/]

only: and ignore: take Regexps, nothing else: watch :docs only: expects a Regexp or an Array of them (got "*.md").

docs.title: Default Ignores
docs.text:
Every watch ignores .git/, coverage/, pkg/, tmp/, log/ and node_modules/ at any depth, so a task that writes its output inside the project never retriggers itself. ignore: adds to that list:

watch :docs, paths: "docs", ignore: %r{\Adrafts/}

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
By default any change counts. events: restricts the kinds:

watch :reindex, paths: "data/**/*.json", events: %i[added removed]   # not on edits
watch :compile, paths: "src", events: :changed                       # edits only

The kinds are :changed, :added and :removed; :modified means :changed. Anything else is rejected: watch :compile events: unknown :edited; use :changed, :added, :removed or :all.

docs.title: Debounce
docs.text:
Saving a file often produces several events in quick succession, and a tool that rewrites many files produces a burst. debounce: is how long the watcher waits after the last event before it runs the task, so the whole burst lands in one run. The default is half a second; raise it for tasks that should see a complete batch:

watch :reindex, paths: "data/**/*.json", events: %i[added removed], debounce: 1

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
env: adds variables to the task's process. The task reads them as usual, with env(:build_env) or ENV["BUILD_ENV"]:

watch :docs, paths: "docs", env: { BUILD_ENV: "dev" }

docs.title: Entry Names
docs.text:
Every declaration is an entry with a name, shown by list and in every log line. The name defaults to the task name. To watch one task from two declarations, give the second an as: name:

watch :lint, paths: "lib/**/*.rb"
watch :lint, paths: "bin/**/*", as: "lint-bin"

Two different declarations with the same name are an error when the .loki loads: watch: "lint" is already declared; give one a distinct as: name. Names may contain letters, digits, _, . and -.

A declaration that names a task the project does not define is caught when the watcher starts: watcher: no such task(s): lintt.

docs.title: Reading the Changes
docs.text:
Inside a task, changes returns what triggered it:

changes.modified   # => ["lib/api.rb"]           paths relative to the project root
changes.added      # => []
changes.removed    # => []
changes.all        # => every path once, in that order
changes.empty?     # => true when the task was run by hand

Every list is empty when the task is run from the command line, so one task body serves both. A lint task that lints only what changed, and everything when nothing is known to have changed:

class Tasks
  desc "Lint the Ruby files that changed, or all of them"
  def lint
    files = changes.modified + changes.added
    files = Dir["lib/**/*.rb"] if files.empty?
    sh "bundle exec rubocop #{files.shelljoin}"
  end

  watch :lint, paths: "lib/**/*.rb"
end

asgard lint              # by hand: lints every file under lib/
echo >> lib/api.rb       # from the watcher: lints lib/api.rb only

Behind changes are three environment variables the watcher sets for the task, ASGARD_MODIFIED, ASGARD_ADDED and ASGARD_REMOVED, one path per line. A shell script run with sh can read them directly. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Managing the Watcher
docs.text:
watcher is also a command with subcommands:

asgard watcher start        # start the watcher for this project in the background
asgard watcher stop         # stop it; a task already running finishes first
asgard watcher list         # this project's watches, daemon state, each entry's last run
asgard watcher list --all   # every project's
asgard watcher preview      # the command and environment each entry would run
asgard watcher log          # print the watcher's log
asgard watcher log -f       # keep following it
asgard watcher run          # watch in the foreground (what start runs detached)

docs.title: start
docs.text:
start launches the watcher as a background process for this project and returns at once:

asgard watcher start

started watcher for api-9f3a1c2b (pid 12345); log: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/watch/api-9f3a1c2b/watcher.log

There is one watcher per project. A second start is refused while the first runs: watcher is already running for api-9f3a1c2b (pid 12345);asgard watcher stopfirst. A pidfile left behind by a crash or a reboot does not count as running; start replaces it.

start refuses when there are no declarations, when a declaration names an unknown task, or when asgard is not on your PATH.

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
stop asks the watcher to finish. It stops listening, drops triggers that have not started, waits for any task that is already running, and then exits. While it waits it names what it is waiting for, once a second:

asgard watcher stop

watcher: waiting for test (pid 12351)
watcher: waiting for test (pid 12351)
stopped watcher for api-9f3a1c2b

stop never signals a running task. A task that hangs keeps stop waiting; kill the task and stop completes. With no watcher running: watcher is not running for api-9f3a1c2b.

docs.title: list
docs.text:
list shows this project's declarations, whether the watcher is running, and each entry's last run:

asgard watcher list

┌──────────┬────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
│ NAME     │ TASK           │ WATCHES                         │ DAEMON  │ LAST RUN                        │
├──────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
│ lint     │ asgard lint    │ lib/**/*.rb                     │ running │ 0 (0.4s, 2026-10-24 09:12:04)   │
│ test     │ asgard test    │ lib test                        │ running │ running (pid 12360)             │
│ docs     │ asgard docs    │ docs                            │ running │ 1 (2.1s, 2026-10-24 09:10:40)   │
│ reindex  │ asgard reindex │ data/**/*.json [added, removed] │ running │ did not finish (pid 12302)      │
│ lint-bin │ asgard lint    │ bin/**/*                        │ running │ never                           │

Logs: /Users/you/.local/state/asgard/watch  (asgard watcher log)
LAST RUN Meaning never The entry has not triggered since records began running (pid N) Its task is running now did not finish (pid N) The task's process is gone but no exit was recorded (a crash, a kill -9) 0 (0.4s, 2026-10-24 09:12:04) The exit status, how long it took, and when it finished

WATCHES lists the declared paths and, when events: restricts the kinds, those kinds in brackets. DAEMON is running or stopped for the whole project.

With no declarations:

No watches declared for api-9f3a1c2b. Add `watch :task, paths: "lib"` inside class Tasks in /Users/you/work/api/.loki.
Use `asgard watcher list --all` to see every project's watches.

list --all (-a) shows every project that has ever started a watcher, each under a Project: slug (/path) title, with [root missing] after a project whose directory no longer exists. Other projects' rows come from the declarations recorded when their watcher was started. Run from a directory with no .loki above it, list shows every project without --all.

docs.title: preview
docs.text:
preview prints, for each entry, the exact command the watcher would run and the complete environment the task would see, without running anything. It is the first thing to look at when a task behaves differently under the watcher than at the prompt.

asgard watcher preview

# lint: /opt/homebrew/bin/direnv exec /Users/you/work/api /Users/you/.gem/bin/asgard lint  (lib/**/*.rb)
ASGARD_ADDED=
ASGARD_MODIFIED=
ASGARD_REMOVED=
ASGARD_WATCH=lint
ASGARD_WATCH_ROOT=/Users/you/work/api
HOME=/Users/you
LANG=en_US.UTF-8
PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
SHELL=/bin/zsh
USER=you

# docs: /opt/homebrew/bin/direnv exec /Users/you/work/api /Users/you/.gem/bin/asgard docs  (docs)
ASGARD_ADDED=
...
BUILD_ENV=dev
...

docs.title: log
docs.text:
The watcher writes one log for the project: a line for every trigger, spawn and exit, with each task's own output in between. log prints it; -f follows it:

asgard watcher log
asgard watcher log -f

Before the first start there is no log: api-9f3a1c2b has no watcher log yet (/Users/you/.local/state/asgard/watch/api-9f3a1c2b/watcher.log); it is created on the first start.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run is the watcher in the foreground: the same process start launches, attached to your terminal instead of detached. It runs until you press Ctrl-C or send it TERM, then shuts down the way stop does and prints watcher: stopped. Use it to see the watcher's own messages as they happen, or as the process a service manager would supervise.

asgard watcher run

docs.title: How Tasks Run
docs.text:
Every trigger starts asgard <task> as a separate process from the project root. The watcher uses the very same asgard executable that started it, by absolute path, so a different version installed elsewhere on PATH is never picked up by accident.

Different tasks run at the same time. A save that matches lint and docs starts both at once.

The same task never overlaps itself. A trigger that arrives while its task is still running waits for it. Several triggers that arrive during one run merge: their changed paths are combined and the task runs once more when the current run ends, with every path from the merged triggers in changes. Save three times during a long test run and one more run follows, not three. The log says so:

2026-10-24 09:12:01 trigger test task=test lib/api.rb
2026-10-24 09:12:01 spawn test task=test pid=12351 lib/api.rb
2026-10-24 09:12:02 trigger test task=test lib/client.rb (queued behind pid 12351)
2026-10-24 09:12:03 trigger test task=test test/api_test.rb (queued behind pid 12351)
2026-10-24 09:12:04 exit test task=test pid=12351 status=0 seconds=3.10
2026-10-24 09:12:04 spawn test task=test pid=12377 lib/client.rb test/api_test.rb
2026-10-24 09:12:07 exit test task=test pid=12377 status=0 seconds=3.02

Each trigger line names the entry and the changed paths. Each spawn and exit line carries the task's pid, so the lines of tasks running side by side can be told apart; a task's own output sits between its spawn and its exit.

Two declarations for the same task (lint and lint-bin above) share one queue, so they never overlap either; a change that matches both runs the task twice, back to back.

A task's depends_on runs inside its own process, as it does from the command line. The watcher does not know about dependencies and does not collapse them across entries.

A task that starts a background job leaves it running after the task exits, and asgard jobs in the project directory shows it.

docs.title: The Environment a Task Sees
docs.text:
The task does not inherit the shell the watcher was started from. It sees the same environment whether the watcher came from an interactive terminal or from a service, which is what makes preview trustworthy.

Layer Contents Base PATH, HOME, USER, LOGNAME, SHELL, LANG, LC_*, TMPDIR, SSH_AUTH_SOCK, and the Ruby setup variables GEM_HOME, GEM_PATH, RUBYOPT, RUBYLIB, BUNDLE_*, captured when the watcher started Declared The entry's env:; the project's .envrc through direnv exec when direnv is on PATH; a .env through the .loki's own dotenv call Trigger ASGARD_WATCH (the entry name), ASGARD_WATCH_ROOT (the project root), and the changed paths in ASGARD_MODIFIED, ASGARD_ADDED and ASGARD_REMOVED, one per line, relative to the root

Nothing else from the daemon reaches the task. A change list too large for the environment (a branch switch under a ** watch can change thousands of files) is written to a file instead, named by ASGARD_CHANGES_FILE; changes reads it the same way.

docs.title: Editing .loki While the Watcher Runs
docs.text:
The watcher watches its own task files too: every .loki the project loaded, and any new .loki that appears in the project root. Save one and the watcher restarts itself with the new declarations once any running task has finished; the log ends one run with watcher: reloading and the next begins. You never need to stop and start after changing a watch line.

If the edited files do not load (a syntax error, a typo), the watcher keeps the declarations it already has and says so in the log:

watcher: the task files do not load; keeping the running declarations

Fix the file and save again.

docs.title: Files and Logs
docs.text:
The watcher keeps everything outside the repository, under ~/.local/state/asgard/watch/<slug>/ (or $XDG_STATE_HOME/asgard/watch/<slug>/), where <slug> is the project directory's name plus a short hash of its full path, api-9f3a1c2b, the same slug scheduled tasks and background jobs use:

File Contents watcher.pid The daemon's pid while it runs watcher.lock Held by the running daemon, so two cannot start watcher.log One line per trigger, spawn and exit, plus every task's output watcher.log.1 The previous log, once watcher.log passed 10 MB (set ASGARD_LOG_MAX in bytes to change the limit) declarations.json The declarations recorded at start, which list --all reads for other projects entries/<name>.json Each entry's last run changes/ Change lists too large for the environment, one file per trigger root The project directory, so list --all can find every project

The directory is readable by you alone, since task output can hold secrets.

docs.title: A Worked Example
docs.text:
The asgard repository ships a small project under examples/watcher_examples/ with four declarations and one placeholder file in each watched directory. Its .loki:

class Tasks
  # A glob: watches lib/ and keeps the paths that match, like a shell would.
  watch :lint, paths: "lib/**/*.rb"

  # A directory with filters. only: narrows to Markdown; ignore: silences
  # the drafts folder; env: adds a variable the task can read with env().
  watch :docs, paths: "docs", only: /\.md\z/, ignore: %r{\Adrafts/}, env: { BUILD_ENV: "demo" }

  # events: picks which kinds of change count. Editing a data file does
  # nothing; creating or deleting one triggers a reindex. debounce: waits
  # a full second after the last event, so a batch of files lands at once.
  watch :reindex, paths: "data/**/*.json", events: %i[added removed], debounce: 1

  # The same task watched from a second declaration needs its own entry
  # name. Both entries share one queue, so lint never overlaps itself.
  watch :lint, paths: "bin/**/*", as: "lint-bin"

  desc "lint", "Report the Ruby files that changed"
  def lint
    files = changes.modified + changes.added
    return puts "lint: nothing changed (run by hand), so linting everything under lib/" if files.empty?

    files.each { |file| puts "lint: #{file} (#{File.foreach(file).count} lines) triggered by #{env(:asgard_watch, 'nothing')}" }
  end

  desc "docs", "Rebuild the documentation"
  def docs
    puts "docs: building for #{env(:build_env, 'development')}; changed: #{changes.all.join(', ')}"
  end

  desc "reindex", "Rebuild the data index"
  def reindex
    puts "reindex: #{changes.added.size} added, #{changes.removed.size} removed; #{Dir['data/**/*.json'].size} data file(s) now"
  end
end

From that directory:

asgard watcher start
echo '# a change' >> lib/greeter.rb         # lint runs, with the path in changes.modified
echo 'more' >> docs/index.md               # docs runs; BUILD_ENV=demo comes from env:
echo 'more' >> docs/drafts/ideas.md        # nothing: drafts/ is ignored
echo '{}' > data/new.json                  # reindex runs: a file was added
echo '{"edited": true}' > data/new.json    # nothing: events: is added and removed only
rm data/new.json                           # reindex runs again: a file was removed
asgard watcher log

Every task also runs by hand, when changes is empty: asgard lint prints lint: nothing changed (run by hand), so linting everything under lib/.

Running the example from a checkout

The watcher runs its daemon and every task as separate asgard processes. If you are running asgard from a git checkout rather than an installed gem, install the checkout first (asgard install from the repository root), or an older gem on the machine may be the one the spawned processes run.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
File events come from the listen gem: native change notifications on macOS and Linux, polling elsewhere. The gem also installs a small native extension, so gem install asgard needs a C++17 compiler on the machine.

Running the watcher as a launchd or systemd service is not built in yet. asgard watcher run is the foreground process such a service would keep alive.

docs.title: Name Collisions
docs.text: The built-in command is registered under a reserved name and mapped to watcher. If your .loki defines its own task called watcher, asgard watcher still runs the built-in; name your task something else. (run is a name Thor uses internally and cannot be a task of yours at all, which is why the foreground command is asgard watcher run and not a task.)
